# Awesome Loop: all deep cards


# LoopRes: Unlocking the Power of Loops in Pretrained LLMs with Loop Residuals

English · [简体中文](../zh/2611.31094.md) · [Back to the list](../../README.md)

<sub>arXiv 2611.31094 · 2026-11-23 · National University of Singapore</sub>


> Finetune a pretrained LLM into a prelude-core-coda loop whose core layers attend over the block outputs of the previous loop, with a trained loop-aware key on each source.

**Category**: Architecture: cross-pass state and residuals · **Status**: draft (numbers not yet re-checked) · **Impact**: cites 0 · stars 71 · HF upvotes 20

[paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.31094) · [code](https://github.com/NUS-HPC-AI-Lab/LoopRes) · [weights](https://huggingface.co/oahzxl/LoopRes-Qwen3-1.7B)

## Problem

Finetuning pretrained LLMs into loops brings only marginal gains over SFT, which the authors attribute to existing designs compressing the outputs of earlier loops into a narrow pathway. Attention Residuals (AttnRes) let layers read earlier outputs directly, but in a loop the sources are iterates of the same layers that look alike, the AttnRes weights settle early in finetuning, and the growing source set lets layers skip intermediate loops.

## Method

- Split the backbone into a prelude, core and coda of one quarter, one half and one quarter of its layers, cut the core into B=2 blocks, and run the core L=3 (2x compute) or L=7 (4x compute) times.
- Inside the core, apply Block AttnRes. Each sub-layer reads a softmax-weighted sum of the prelude output, earlier block outputs and the current block's partial sum, with its own zero-initialized query in each loop.
- Give each source a trainable loop-aware key, one vector per block per loop initialized from N(0, I), scored by a second query and added to the score of the RMSNorm content key.
- Keep only the block outputs of the latest W=1 loops as sources, so each input has at most (W+1)B+1 sources, and fuse the read into one Triton kernel.

## Loop layout

| Facet | Value |
|---|---|
| Where the loop sits | middle core (prelude-core-coda) |
| Weight sharing | fully tied |
| Passes in training | fixed |
| Passes at test time | fixed |
| Input injection | attention over earlier passes |
| KV cache | per-pass KV |
| Gradient through passes | full BPTT |
| Origin | retrofitted from a pretrained model |
| FFN | dense FFN |
| Attention in the loop | full attention |
| Passes (L7-20) | train 3 or 7; test 3 or 7 |

Shown is Qwen3-1.7B-Base (28 layers). Every backbone is split into a prelude, core and coda of one quarter, one half and one quarter of its layers, and the core is cut into B=2 blocks. Running the core L=3 or L=7 times costs 2x or 4x the backbone's compute, measured in layers passed per token; each loop count is a separately trained model. Inside the core, every sub-layer reads a softmax mix of the prelude output, the block outputs of the previous W=1 loop, the finished blocks of the current loop and the current block's partial sum, instead of the residual stream. The prelude and coda keep the standard residual stream.

## Results

| BRT | 49.2 \| 0.302 |

## Other findings

- With plain AttnRes in the looped core, the weight on the path through every loop falls from 33.7% with three loops to 0.05% with seven, and the most likely paths never reach the later loops. (Section 2.3; Figure 2e)
- In the learned weights, the first core block mainly updates its own output from the previous loop, and the second block relies most on the first block of the current loop. (Section 3.5; Figure 6a,b)
- Shapley values attribute most of the source selection to the loop-aware key at both compute budgets, with a smaller share for the content key. (Section 3.5; Figure 6c)
- The content key steers simple tokens such as "But" and "Wait" toward shallower outputs, and digits and math symbols toward deeper ones. (Section 3.5; Figure 6d)
- Under AttnRes the content score is almost a fixed preference over sources and barely varies with the token; under LoopRes it varies far more with the token, even as loops deepen. (Section 3.5; Figure 7c,d)
- Scores rise with loop depth and saturate beyond L=5; the authors pick L=3 as the best trade-off between score and compute. (Section 3.3; Figure 5; Table 10)
- On the five harder benchmarks, LoopRes on Qwen3-4B-Base (45.8) scores above SFT on Qwen3-8B-Base (42.9). (Section 3.3; Table 3)

## Comparison

- **Baseline**: SFT (the same backbone finetuned without looping) and 8 looped designs reimplemented on the same backbone and finetuned on the same data with the same hyperparameters. Ouro, TaH2-fixed, CloseLoop, InfiLoop and BRT loop all layers (L=2 and 4); Huginn, Hyperloop and WMRE loop the middle half, as LoopRes does (L=3 and 7).
- **Held fixed**: N (unique parameters), D (training tokens)
- **Differs**: F (training FLOPs), L (executed layers per token), KV (KV cache per token)
- **Baseline hyperparameters**: shared with the looped model
- **Headline claim**: On Qwen3-1.7B-Base at 2x compute, LoopRes raises the average of seven math and code scores from 43.2 (SFT) to 55.8, a 29.1% gain, against 49.2 (13.9%) for the strongest baseline, BRT. At 4x compute it reaches 57.8 (33.7%), against 51.8 (19.8%) for Huginn. (Abstract; Table 1)

## Caveats

- Finetuning only. The 1.7B runs use 572K math and code conversations (3.1B tokens) for 12,000 steps on 16,384-token sequences, evaluation covers math and code benchmarks only, and the authors say broader tasks and RL remain untested.
- Compute is not matched against SFT; LoopRes passes 2x or 4x the backbone's layers per token, and the looped baselines are compared at the same 2x and 4x. LoopRes adds per-loop query and key vectors, and the paper prints no parameter counts.
- The paper reports no KV cache sizes; the official code caches keys and values for every (layer, loop step) pass.
- No run applies AttnRes or LoopRes without looping. The closest control for the residual change is Huginn with and without AttnRes on the same looped core (Tables 1 and 5).
- All models share one hyperparameter set (learning rate 3e-5, picked from a five-value sweep, Appendix A.4); the baselines are not tuned separately.
- Baselines are reimplemented as finetunes of the same backbone with changes, such as Ouro without its exit gate, Huginn with a fixed loop count and Parcae's diagonal injection, InfiLoop with a single running average and BRT with seven blocks of four layers; six of the originals pretrain from scratch (Appendix A.2).
- Every token runs all L loops in training and at inference.

## Open questions stated by the authors

- Can combining LoopRes with reinforcement learning cut the rollout budget, given its lower cost of matching SFT on long outputs?
- Can the model decide how many loops each token or sequence needs?
- The loop-depth scaling curve has not saturated on larger backbones; how does looping behave at greater scale?
- The learned loop dependencies follow clear patterns; could a simpler, fixed connection scheme capture most of the benefit without learned attention weights?

## Reproducibility

|---|---|---|---|
| available | partial | partial | available |

## Related open questions

- [Where in the stack should the loop sit?](questions.md#loop-placement) (supports)

## Authors

Xuanlei Zhao, Hailun Xu, Kai Wang, Yang Luo, Yingxuan Ren, Zirui Zhu, Yuxuan Lou, Kun Xu, Yan Wang, Kanchan Sarkar, Yang You


# GLM-5.4: GLM-5.4: Toward Generalized Coding with Our First Loop Transformer

English · [简体中文](../zh/zai-glm-5-4.md) · [Back to the list](../../README.md)

<sub>Z.ai blog · 2026-11-23 · Z.ai</sub>


> Z.ai turns 28 layers of its pre-trained GLM-5 base into a two-pass loop through continued training at the 750B scale, with per-token gates, a shared-plus-sliding-window KV cache and reused sparse-attention indices.

**Category**: Training and retrofitting · **Status**: draft (numbers not yet re-checked) · **Impact**: HN points 1,180

[paper](https://z.ai/blog/glm-5.4)

## Problem

Long-chain tasks such as large-scale software engineering, 3D modeling and physical control need more effective compute per token, but looped models trained from scratch lag behind unshared models at the same pre-training compute.

## Method

- Adapt the pre-trained GLM-5 base into a Loop Transformer by continued training, running 28 weight-shared layers for two iterations.
- Add independent per-token gates for each iteration that write candidate updates back into the residual stream, so activation norms stay stable.
- Let the second loop reuse the first pass's sparse KV and attention indices plus its own sliding-window KV, and fuse kernels to cut intermediate memory traffic.

## Loop layout

| Facet | Value |
|---|---|
| Where the loop sits | middle core (prelude-core-coda) |
| Weight sharing | fully tied |
| Passes in training | fixed |
| Passes at test time | fixed |
| Input injection | gated |
| KV cache | first-pass KV shared |
| Gradient through passes | n/a |
| Origin | retrofitted from a pretrained model |
| FFN | n/a |
| Attention in the loop | hybrid (full + window / linear) |
| Passes (28 shared layers) | train 2; test 2 |

GLM-5.4 loops 28 layers of the GLM-5 base model for two iterations; the post describes them as middle layers but does not give the base model's layer count or which 28 layers are looped. The loop was added to the already pre-trained base through continued training at the 750B scale.

## Results

**30B, same architecture as the 750B base, iso-parameter, about 10% more total training compute; after 200K long-context SFT, thinking mode on** · score, baseline / + Loop · Scaling Correctness & Controlled Iso-Parameter Ablations (results table)

| Variant | Value |
|---|---|
| AIME25 | 19.17 / 30.42 |
| GPQA-Diamond | 47.58 / 56.26 |
| AA-LCR | 40.33 / 47.67 |
| MMLU-Pro | 71.65 / 75.05 |
| IFBench | 50.20 / 53.47 |

**Same 30B comparison** · average output length change with the loop · Scaling Correctness & Controlled Iso-Parameter Ablations (results table)

| Variant | Value |
|---|---|
| AIME25 | -635 tokens (-2%) |
| GPQA-Diamond | -2,473 tokens (-11.7%) |
| AA-LCR | -539 tokens (-9.7%) |
| MMLU-Pro | -863 tokens (-14.9%) |
| IFBench | -763 tokens (-13.0%) |

**GLM-5.4 serving** · output speed · Inference Efficiency

| Variant | Value |
|---|---|
| Off-peak | up to 200 tokens/s |
| Peak load | 70-80 tokens/s |

## Other findings

- Converting middle layers of a pre-trained model into a loop by directly overwriting hidden states makes activation norms blow up across iterations; per-token gates for each iteration fix this, with the first pass writing conservatively and the second pass opening the gates, and harder tokens getting larger first-pass writes. (Gated Progressive Updates)
- The second loop reuses the sparse KV selected in the first pass and keeps only its own new KV in a sliding window, so an extra loop costs one sliding window of KV rather than a full context cache. (Hybrid KV Cache (Global Sharing + Independent Sliding Window))
- Reusing the first loop's sparse-attention indices in the second loop performs nearly identically to recomputing them on every pass. (Sparse Attention Index Reuse)
- The authors state that looped models trained from scratch still lag behind unshared models under the same pre-training compute budget, which is why they adapted a pre-trained base through continued training instead. (From Pre-Trained Base to Loop Transformer)

## Comparison

- **Baseline**: A 30B model with the same architecture as the 750B base, without the loop, evaluated after 200K long-context SFT with thinking mode enabled.
- **Held fixed**: N (unique parameters)
- **Differs**: F (training FLOPs)
- **Baseline hyperparameters**: not stated
- **Headline claim**: With identical parameter counts and about 10% more total training compute, the looped 30B model improves AIME25 from 19.17 to 30.42 and GPQA-Diamond from 47.58 to 56.26, while average output length drops by 10-14% on most benchmarks. (Scaling Correctness & Controlled Iso-Parameter Ablations (results table))

## Caveats

- This is a blog post, not a paper; the base model's layer count, which 28 layers are looped, the training tokens and the evaluation details beyond the table are not given.
- The controlled comparison is iso-parameter, not iso-compute (the looped 30B model used about 10% more total training compute), and it is reported only at 30B after long-context SFT; the 750B results are not shown as a controlled comparison.
- The claim that GLM-5.4 reaches intelligence levels comparable to 2T-3T parameter models comes without a stated evaluation protocol in the post.
- The authors note that the model tends to get caught in overly long "marathon thinking" loops.
- Weights are not released yet (planned after safety hardening) and the API is listed as coming soon.

## Open questions stated by the authors

- How to make compute adaptive so that harder tokens get more iterations.
- How the returns of looping behave as both loop count and model size keep growing.

## Reproducibility

| Code | Weights | Configs | Data |
|---|---|---|---|
| none | none | none | none |

## Authors

Z.ai


# Inkling 2 Mini: Introducing Inkling 2 Mini

English · [简体中文](../zh/tml-inkling-2-mini.md) · [Back to the list](../../README.md)

<sub>Thinking Machines Lab blog · 2026-11-20 · Thinking Machines Lab</sub>


> Open-weight MoE (26.4B total, 3.4B active) that runs the middle 12 of its 24 layers three times with shared weights, released with a variable-loop research twin used to measure how pass count affects capability and CoT monitorability.

**Category**: Architecture: where to loop, what to share · **Status**: draft (numbers not yet re-checked) · **Impact**: HN points 1,488

[paper](https://thinkingmachines.ai/news/inkling-2-mini/) · [project](https://thinkingmachines.ai/model-card/inkling-2-mini/) · [blog](https://huggingface.co/blog/inkling2mini) · [weights](https://huggingface.co/thinkingmachines/Inkling-2-Mini)

## Problem

Looping lets a model do more serial computation per token without adding parameters, which has raised concerns that looped models are harder to oversee by reading their chain of thought; the post reports what looping gives a small open model and how pass count affects CoT monitorability.

## Method

- 24 MoE layers (8 of 128 experts per token) in four six-layer blocks; the two middle blocks share weights and run three times, giving 48 layer applications per token from 24 stored layers.
- Every pass starts from the prelude output; passes 2 and 3 also read the previous pass's middle-block outputs (the message) through attention residuals, and a learned gate that initially blocks the message lets looping be introduced stably during training.
- Training started with 8 of 384 experts per token; two-thirds of the experts were pruned at one point in midtraining (keeping the 128 most used per layer), followed by 1T tokens distilled from a larger internal Inkling model, SFT, and RL totaling 2.2T tokens over 2,000 steps. Expert layers use NVFP4 on all forward passes and the last four layers use MXFP8.
- A variable-loop research model, TML-d24-varloop-research, was trained with 1 to 5 passes (sampled 1:2:6:2:1 for the rest of midtraining, post-trained at 3) and is run at 1 to 5 passes, and at 10 in the no-CoT tests, to measure capability and CoT monitorability.

## Loop layout

| Facet | Value |
|---|---|
| Where the loop sits | middle core (prelude-core-coda) |
| Weight sharing | fully tied |
| Passes in training | fixed |
| Passes at test time | fixed |
| Input injection | attention over earlier passes |
| KV cache | per-pass KV |
| Gradient through passes | n/a |
| Origin | n/a |
| FFN | MoE |
| Attention in the loop | hybrid (full + window / linear) |
| Passes (L6-17) | train 3; test 3 |

Inkling 2 Mini has 24 MoE layers (8 of 128 experts per token) in four six-layer blocks; the two middle blocks share weights and run three times, so 24 stored layers give 48 layer applications per token. Per the Hugging Face blog, each block has five sliding-window layers (1,024-token window) and one full-attention layer, and each layer visit keeps its own KV. Every pass starts from the prelude output; passes 2 and 3 also read the previous pass's middle-block outputs (the message) through attention residuals, admitted by a learned gate that starts fully closed. Labels are 0-indexed as in the Hugging Face blog; the post numbers the same core 7-18. The released research twin TML-d24-varloop-research has the same layout but was trained with 1 to 5 passes and is run at up to 10 in the post.

## Results

**Scaling-ladder runs at training step 2,000, three passes, equal training compute; range over three evaluations** · compute a no-loop baseline is estimated to need to match the looped run's loss · Looping design; figure "Compute-equivalent gain by loop position"

| Variant | Value |
|---|---|
| Loop middle layers (7–18) | 1.51–1.91× |
| Loop last layers (13–24) | 1.24–1.36× |

**Subset of Think Fast tasks, no-CoT answers elicited by prefilling the response; Varloop = TML-d24-varloop-research, trained with 1-5 passes** · no-CoT 50% time horizon (human seconds) · No-CoT capabilities; figure "No-CoT time horizons"

| Variant | Value |
|---|---|
| Inkling 2 Mini, 3 passes | 41 s |
| Varloop, 1 pass | 16 s |
| Varloop, 2 passes | 26 s |
| Varloop, 3 passes | 37 s |
| Varloop, 5 passes | 42 s |
| Varloop, 10 passes | 40 s |

**TML-d24-varloop-research run at 1-5 passes (1-5 passes sampled 1:2:6:2:1 for the rest of midtraining, post-trained at 3)** · score at 1 / 2 / 3 / 4 / 5 passes · TML-d24-varloop-research model card, Section 5 (Evaluations)

| Variant | Value |
|---|---|
| DeepSWE v1.1 (mini-swe-agent v2.4.6) | 0.7% / 28.3% / 47.4% / 46.9% / 48.2% |
| GPQA Diamond | 69.6% / 79.2% / 84.2% / 81.9% / 83.1% |
| MRCR v2 8-needle 256K–512K | 26.2% / 65.2% / 89.2% / 93.4% / 92.1% |
| SimpleQA Verified | 6.3% / 6.5% / 7.3% / 6.8% / 6.7% |

**TML-d24-varloop-research on the GPQA Diamond questions it answered correctly at all five pass counts** · mean reasoning tokens / mean words per sentence / words in an English dictionary / uncertainty indicators · CoT monitorability; Compression and legibility table

| Variant | Value |
|---|---|
| 1 pass | 3703 / 8.9 / 94.6% / 9.7 |
| 3 passes | 1731 / 8.7 / 94.5% / 3.9 |
| 5 passes | 1661 / 8.7 / 94.4% / 3.6 |

**LinuxArena, subset of 184 main-task/side-task pairings, simple-attack policy, monitor Qwen3.6-35B-A3B at a 1% false-positive rate; Inkling 2 Mini is a helpful-only fine-tune; Varloop = TML-d24-varloop-research** · stealth rate (% of attack episodes), monitor sees tool calls and outputs only / also sees text and thinking · Agentic monitorability; figure "LinuxArena stealth rate"

| Variant | Value |
|---|---|
| Inkling 2 Mini (helpful-only) | 3.9% / 1.3% |
| Varloop, 1 pass | 1.0% / 0.3% |
| Varloop, 2 passes | 2.5% / 0.4% |
| Varloop, 3 passes | 4.0% / 0.6% |
| Varloop, 4 passes | 2.8% / 0.3% |
| Varloop, 5 passes | 5.0% / 0.0% |

## Other findings

- On the scaling ladder, an unpruned non-looping model cost 7.5% less compute to train than the unpruned looped version but needed 140% more inference compute to match its loss on 512k-token agentic traces. (Looping design)
- TML-d24-varloop-research was never trained with more than five passes, yet running it with ten does not significantly degrade its no-CoT time horizon (40 s, against 42 s at five), and on N-Hop Lookup it follows longer chains with more passes, improving out to ten loops. (No-CoT capabilities; figures "No-CoT time horizons" and "N-Hop Lookup")
- With CoT, more passes mainly help multi-hop reasoning rather than recall: gains are largest on long-context retrieval (MRCR), then math and science reasoning, then long-horizon agentic tasks, while knowledge-intensive benchmarks (AA-Omniscience, SimpleQA Verified, SimpleVQA, WorldVQA) do not improve with more passes. (Capabilities; No-CoT capabilities)
- Accuracy at each reasoning-token budget generally rises with passes, with diminishing returns after 3; on GPQA Diamond questions solved at all pass counts, reasoning at 5 passes averages 1,661 tokens against 3,703 at 1 pass, with unchanged sentence length and dictionary-word share. (CoT monitorability; Compression and legibility)
- Among CoTs of 750-1,250 tokens, Inkling 2 Mini and the variable-loop model at 3 passes follow a CoT instruction at most 0.1% of the time (Qwen3.8-27B 1.3%), too rarely to separate loop counts; LinuxArena stealth rates show no clear trend with the number of passes. (CoT monitorability (Controllability); Agentic monitorability)

## Comparison

- **Baseline**: A scaling-ladder run that loops the last 12 layers (13-24) instead of the middle 12 (7-18), with the same three passes and equal training compute; both runs' gains are expressed as the compute a no-loop baseline would need to match their loss.
- **Held fixed**: F (training FLOPs)
- **Differs**: none
- **Baseline hyperparameters**: not stated
- **Headline claim**: Looping the middle 12 layers gave larger accuracy gains than looping the last 12 on 27 of 28 evaluations; at training step 2,000 a no-loop baseline was estimated to need 1.51-1.91x the compute to match the middle loop's loss, against 1.24-1.36x for the last loop. (Looping design; figure "Compute-equivalent gain by loop position")

## Caveats

- Inkling 2 Mini supports only a fixed number of passes (3), so every pass-count comparison uses TML-d24-varloop-research, whose later training stages differ; its model card cautions against comparing it directly with Inkling 2 Mini.
- Three passes dominated the variable-loop model's training and its RL used 3 passes only; the authors say results at other pass counts may understate what dedicated training could achieve and do not show what RL at a higher pass count would learn.
- The loop-placement and looping-versus-non-looping comparisons come from scaling-ladder runs (placement at training step 2,000; unpruned models for looping versus non-looping), not from the released model, and the post does not give the sizes of those runs.
- No-CoT results use a subset of Think Fast tasks, with answers elicited by prefilling the start of the response; the models were not trained to answer without CoT.
- LinuxArena used a helpful-only fine-tune of Inkling 2 Mini, a weaker monitor (Qwen3.6-35B-A3B) and a subset of 184 task pairings.
- Decoding speeds in the opening coding figure are theoretical ceilings (614 GB/s, BF16 weights, batch size one), evaluation setups vary by model, and the post gives no pretraining token count.

# Looped CED: Looping Deeper Without Growing the KV Cache: Recurrent Depth for Causal Encoder-Decoders

English · [简体中文](../zh/2611.13378.md) · [Back to the list](../../README.md)

<sub>arXiv 2611.13378 · 2026-11-09 · University of California, San Diego, Tsinghua University, Nanjing University</sub>


> Loop the CED encoder layers that produce global KV, train with random depth, and keep only the last round's KV.

**Category**: Architecture: where to loop, what to share · **Status**: draft (numbers not yet re-checked) · **Impact**: cites 0

[paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.13378)

## Problem

When every round caches its own KV, a looped model's KV cache grows with the number of rounds, which cancels the memory advantage of KV-sparse layouts such as the causal encoder-decoder.

## Method

- Loop layers L2-5 of the encoder, which contain its only global KV source, for 8 rounds with Parcae's gated input injection.
- Sample the number of rounds per sequence from max(1, Poisson(8)) and backpropagate through the last 4, so the core settles into a fixed point.
- At inference, past tokens keep only their last-round KV, so the resident KV equals the unlooped CED's.

## Loop layout

| Facet | Value |
|---|---|
| Where the loop sits | KV-producing half (CED encoder / YOCO self-decoder) |
| Weight sharing | fully tied |
| Passes in training | sampled |
| Passes at test time | can run more passes than trained |
| Input injection | gated |
| KV cache | last-pass KV only |
| Gradient through passes | truncated (last k passes) |
| Origin | trained from scratch |
| FFN | dense FFN |
| Attention in the loop | hybrid (full + window / linear) |
| Passes (L2-5) | train max(1, Poisson(8)); test 8 |
| Backprop (L2-5) | last 4 |

12-layer causal encoder-decoder (CED) in the DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash layout: every layer has SWA-128; L2 is the encoder's only global KV source and L6 projects the global KV shared by the decoder. The loop repeats L2-5.

## Results

**150M non-embedding params, 6.0B tokens, FineWeb-Edu, 2048 context, T=8 at evaluation** · validation BPB (lower is better) · Table 1

| Variant | Value |
|---|---|
| Dense, no loop | 0.8747 |
| Dense, loop L2-5 | 0.8461 |
| CED, no loop | 0.8716 |
| CED, encoder loop L2-5 | 0.8468 |
| CED, decoder loop L7-10 | 0.8648 |
| CED, encoder loop, fixed rounds | 0.8487 |
| YOCO-U style, loop L2-5 | 0.8506 |

**150M, 29.6B tokens** · validation BPB / DCLM CORE accuracy · Table 2

| Variant | Value |
|---|---|
| CED, no loop | 0.8401 / 19.09 |
| CED, encoder loop | 0.8124 / 21.63 |
| CED, decoder loop | 0.8295 / 21.56 |

**150M, 6.0B tokens, exact fp32 token-by-token decoding at T=8** · BPB with last-round KV minus BPB with per-round KV · Table 3

| Variant | Value |
|---|---|
| Encoder loop, stochastic depth | -0.0002 |
| Encoder loop, fixed depth | +0.0317 |

**DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash (552B) looped for 8 rounds on 4x GB200, serving only (no loop training)** · KV per token and 128K-token requests that fit · Abstract; Table 4

| Variant | Value |
|---|---|
| Per-layer and per-round KV | cannot fit one 128K request |
| Looped CED (last-round KV) | 36.8x less KV per token, fits 38 requests |

## Other findings

- Running 12 or 16 rounds instead of the trained mean of 8 lowers BPB by at most 0.0004 and never raises it. (Appendix F; Table 9)
- After 5x longer training (29.6B tokens) the decoder loop still captures only 38% of the encoder loop's improvement. (Table 2)

## Comparison

- **Baseline**: Unlooped CED with the same 12-layer layout; dense, decoder-loop and YOCO-U-style variants are also compared.
- **Held fixed**: N (unique parameters), D (training tokens), KV (KV cache per token)
- **Differs**: F (training FLOPs), L (executed layers per token)
- **Baseline hyperparameters**: shared with the looped model
- **Headline claim**: At 150M, the encoder loop lowers BPB from 0.8716 to 0.8468 while keeping the unlooped CED's 8 KB of global KV per token; the paper reports recovering 86-93% of a looped Transformer's gain with 1/6 of its global KV. (Abstract; Table 1)

## Caveats

- Training experiments use 12-layer dense-FFN models up to 340M non-embedding parameters at 2K context; the 552B DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash runs measure serving cost only, with no loop training.
- Parameters, tokens and KV are held fixed but compute is not; a looped model runs 40 layer passes per decoded token instead of 12.
- All runs share one hyperparameter set (Table 8); the baselines were not tuned separately.
- The encoder loop puts every round on the prefill path; in the 552B serving test, prefill cost per prompt token at T=8 is 5.12x the unlooped CED (Table 13).

## Reproducibility

| Code | Weights | Configs | Data |
|---|---|---|---|
| none | none | partial | available |

## Related open questions

- [Does running more passes at test time than in training keep improving quality?](questions.md#extra-passes-at-test-time) (partly)
- [Where in the stack should the loop sit?](questions.md#loop-placement) (supports)
- [Can later passes reuse one KV cache instead of keeping KV for every pass?](questions.md#shared-kv-across-passes) (partly)

## Authors

Jiaqi Leng, Minshen Zhang, Zhaofeng Sun, Yu-Yang Qian, Peng Zhao, Hao Zhang


# LoopDuet: Not All Loops Cost the Same: Phase-Dependent Depth for Serving Looped Transformers

English · [简体中文](../zh/2611.07211.md) · [Back to the list](../../README.md)

<sub>arXiv 2611.07211 · 2026-11-04 · Duke University</sub>


> Serve looped Transformers with fewer core loops for ordinary prompt tokens than for the last prompt token and the decoded tokens, run the deep tail as a compact batch in vLLM, and lower prefilling depth when the queue grows.

**Category**: Systems and inference · **Status**: draft (numbers not yet re-checked) · **Impact**: cites 1

[paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.07211)

## Problem

Serving a looped model with one loop count for all tokens ties prefill cost to decode depth. With long prompts and short answers (OLMo HotpotQA prompts average 796 tokens and answers about 4.7), prompt positions account for over 99% of layer applications, so keeping deep decoding repeats deep computation over the whole prompt.

## Method

- Choose decode depth S and prefill depth P <= S jointly from measured quality-throughput trade-offs; ordinary prompt positions stop after P core loops, while every prompt-chunk endpoint and every decoded token runs S.
- In vLLM, after P loops the engine gathers each request's final query into a compact B x d batch for the remaining S - P loops and scatters it back before the coda; prompt context stays in one shared KV plane per core layer, so existing weights and attention kernels are reused.
- A queue-age controller maps the oldest first-token wait from 0.25 s to 1 s linearly onto [P_min, P_max] before each engine step, keeping S fixed (main setting S = 4, P in {2, 3, 4}).
- A recurrent-state distance (90th percentile over ordinary prompt tokens, threshold about 0.24) screens candidate P values before task-accuracy checks.

## Loop layout

| Facet | Value |
|---|---|
| Where the loop sits | middle core (prelude-core-coda) |
| Weight sharing | fully tied |
| Passes in training | n/a |
| Passes at test time | adaptive exit / routing |
| Input injection | n/a |
| KV cache | last-pass KV only |
| Gradient through passes | n/a |
| Origin | n/a |
| FFN | dense FFN |
| Attention in the loop | full attention |
| Passes (R6) | train 32 (OLMo r32 checkpoint); test S for decode, P <= S for prefill, at most 32 |

Shown for OLMo r32, a recurrent OLMo-2 retrofit with 4/6/4 prelude/core/coda layers at width 2,048 (the r16 checkpoint has the same layout and was trained at 16 loops); Huginn-0125 has 2/4/2 layers at width 5,280. LoopDuet trains nothing. Ordinary prompt positions run P core loops, while every prompt-chunk endpoint and every decoded token runs S. Serving keeps one shared KV plane per core layer that each loop overwrites, so later queries read the last computed KV of positions that stopped early.

## Results

**Huginn-0125, full HotpotQA distractor dev set (7,405 examples), one A100-SXM4-80GB, vLLM 0.14.1, bf16, no prefix caching, C = 64** · throughput (req/s) / EM · Table A6; Figure 3

| Variant | Value |
|---|---|
| Uniform (32, 32) | 0.976 / 33.79 |
| Uniform (20, 20) | 1.536 / 33.52 |
| Uniform (16, 16) | 1.897 / 32.07 |
| Uniform (8, 8) | 3.587 / 24.29 |
| LoopDuet (32, 16) | 1.822 / 33.69 |
| LoopDuet (14, 8) | 3.489 / 30.33 |

**Same HotpotQA serving setup, OLMo r32 with four-paragraph prompts** · throughput (req/s) / EM · Table A6; Figure A1

| Variant | Value |
|---|---|
| Uniform (32, 32) | 9.156 / 38.49 |
| Uniform (11, 11) | 24.302 / 38.43 |
| Uniform (8, 8) | 32.220 / 38.37 |
| Uniform (4, 4) | 56.464 / 37.95 |
| LoopDuet (32, 8) | 27.315 / 38.42 |
| LoopDuet (11, 4) | 51.850 / 38.27 |

**HotpotQA, C = 64; each LoopDuet setting against a uniform setting whose throughput differs by at most 10%** · throughput ratio LoopDuet/uniform / ΔEM / ΔF1 · Table 1

| Variant | Value |
|---|---|
| Huginn (14, 8) vs (8, 8) | 0.973 / +6.04 / +7.13 |
| Huginn (24, 12) vs (12, 12) | 0.979 / -0.45 / -0.47 |
| Huginn (32, 16) vs (16, 16) | 0.960 / +1.62 / +1.90 |
| Huginn (32, 16) vs (18, 18) | 1.073 / +0.97 / +1.10 |
| OLMo r32 (11, 4) vs (4, 4) | 0.918 / +0.32 / +0.49 |

**HotpotQA, C = 64, decoding depth S held fixed; LoopDuet (S, P) against uniform (S, S)** · speedup / EM uniform → LoopDuet / measured speedup as a fraction of the layer-pass ratio · Table A7; Figure 4

| Variant | Value |
|---|---|
| OLMo r32 (32, 8) | 2.98× / 38.49 → 38.42 / 85% |
| OLMo r32 (11, 4) | 2.13× / 38.43 → 38.27 / 93% |
| Huginn (32, 16) | 1.87× / 33.79 → 33.69 / 96% |

**OLMo r32, S = 4, all HotpotQA examples, open-loop C = 128; queue controller with P in [2, 4]** · one-second TTFT attainment (%) / EM · Table 2

| Variant | Value |
|---|---|
| Poisson 60 req/s, fixed (4, 4) | 8.6 / 38.04 |
| Poisson 60 req/s, fixed (4, 3) | 100 / 36.35 |
| Poisson 60 req/s, LoopDuet queue | 100 / 37.27 |
| Burst 10/60 req/s, fixed (4, 4) | 46.9 / 38.04 |
| Burst 10/60 req/s, fixed (4, 3) | 100 / 36.42 |
| Burst 10/60 req/s, LoopDuet queue | 100 / 37.77 |
| Burst 20/80 req/s, fixed (4, 2) | 100 / 31.91 |
| Burst 20/80 req/s, LoopDuet queue | 87.5 / 35.12 |

**GSM8K, all 1,319 test examples, five demonstrations, greedy decoding; changes from each checkpoint's (S, S) control** · accuracy change (pp), uniform (P, P) / LoopDuet (S, P) · Figure 6; Section 4.5

| Variant | Value |
|---|---|
| Huginn, (S, P) = (14, 8) | -10.99 / +0.68 |
| OLMo r16, (S, P) = (16, 4) | -1.44 / +1.74 |
| OLMo r32, (S, P) = (11, 4) | -4.85 / +1.06 |

## Other findings

- The first output token needs full depth: for Huginn on HotpotQA at S = 32 with other prompt positions at P = 16, running the final prompt position at 16 loops instead of 32 lowers EM by 1.74 points relative to (32, 16) and by 1.97 points relative to (32, 32). (Section 4.5)
- Split budgets do not always win: Huginn (24, 12) gives 31.60 EM at 2.43 req/s, while uniform (12, 12) gives 32.05 EM at 2.48 req/s. (Section 4.2; Table 1)
- For OLMo r32 on HotpotQA, EM stays between 37.95 and 38.49 across all six tested settings, so uniform depth four, the fastest at 56.46 req/s and 0.54 points below (32, 32), is chosen as the controller's starting point. (Section 4.2; Figure A1; Table A6)
- Useful prefilling depth is task dependent: on ARC at S = 11, raising OLMo r32's P from 4 to 8 moves the accuracy change from -1.54 to +0.85 points, and Huginn (14, 8) stays 4.44 points below (14, 14). (Section 4.5; Figure 8)
- The savings survive batching: Huginn (32, 16) keeps 1.84x, 1.87x and 1.88x speedups over (32, 32) at engine-step token budgets of 4,096, 8,192 and 16,384 (C = 128), and 1.87x at C = 32, 64 and 128. (Section 4.3; Table A9)

## Comparison

- **Baseline**: Uniform-depth serving (S, S) of the same checkpoint in the same vLLM engine, with the same prompts, KV layout, precision and execution mode; (32, 32) is the full-depth reference, and fixed prefilling depths at the same S are the controls under load.
- **Held fixed**: N (unique parameters), D (training tokens), KV (KV cache per token)
- **Differs**: L (executed layers per token), W (wall-clock time)
- **Baseline hyperparameters**: shared with the looped model
- **Headline claim**: On full HotpotQA with one A100-80GB, Huginn (32, 16) gives 1.19x the throughput of (20, 20), the fastest tested uniform setting meeting the same accuracy criterion, and (14, 8) gains 6.04 EM points over uniform (8, 8) at 97% of its throughput. Under load, adapting OLMo's prefilling depth gains 0.92-1.35 EM points over the most accurate tested fixed depths at the same 100% one-second TTFT attainment. (Abstract; Figure 3; Table 1; Table 2)

## Caveats

- Training-free serving study of existing checkpoints only (Huginn-0125 and the recurrent OLMo-2 retrofits r16 and r32); every tested depth is at most 32 loops (16 for OLMo r16).
- Tasks are GSM8K, HotpotQA (distractor dev set) and ARC-Challenge, with model-specific prompts (OLMo four paragraphs and one demonstration under a 1,000-token cap; Huginn ten paragraphs and two demonstrations); the authors call these within-model comparisons, not a ranking between models.
- All timings use one A100-SXM4-80GB, vLLM 0.14.1, bf16 and no prefix caching; the joint-depth comparison uses one execution per configuration at C = 64.
- Gains depend on the workload: on GSM8K, longer responses give wall-time ratios of 0.98-1.01 across four serving pairs despite layer-pass ratios of 1.52-2.71.
- Decoding reads prompt KV from the last loop each position computed, an approximation to full-depth context that the authors evaluate through task accuracy; the controller has no correctness feedback and works within a depth range chosen offline.
- On the 20/80 req/s burst trace the controller reaches 87.5% one-second TTFT attainment, against 100% for fixed P = 2.

## Reproducibility

|---|---|---|---|
| none | none | partial | available |

## Authors

Zhixu Du, Yuhan Cheng, Hai (Helen) Li, Yiran Chen


# SMELT: SMELT: Scaling Laws for Compute-Matched MoE Looped Transformers

English · [简体中文](../zh/2609.01343.md) · [Back to the list](../../README.md)

<sub>arXiv 2609.01343 · 2026-09-01 · Tsinghua University, ByteDance Seed, M-A-P, TokenWave.AI</sub>


> With per-token FLOPs, total parameters and KV cache matched, looping the middle half of an MoE Transformer twice lowers loss at four scales up to 54B non-embedding parameters and saves 6.8-18.0% of training FLOPs on the fitted frontier.

**Category**: Scaling and budget · **Status**: draft (numbers not yet re-checked) · **Impact**: cites 35 · HF upvotes 91

[paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.01343)

## Problem

Most looped-model gains are reported at fixed parameter count, where the looped model also spends more FLOPs and KV cache, so architecture and extra compute are conflated; the paper asks whether looping still helps when per-token FLOPs, total parameters and KV cache are all held fixed.

## Method

- Pay for the extra pass by narrowing the hidden size (1280 to 1056 at 200M, S ≈ 95%), recover total parameters by adding experts (192 to 288 per layer), and use smaller heads at a higher GQA ratio to keep the KV cache within 4%.
- Choose the recipe with three 200M ablations under these budgets; loop the middle 50% of layers twice, keep the Baseline's physical depth, and scale each looped sublayer's residual update by 1/r.
- Train matched Baseline / SMELT pairs over 4 scales x 4 sparsity levels with six WSD decay branches each (up to about 215B tokens), and fit a separate Chinchilla-style law L(F, S, D) per architecture to compare compute-optimal frontiers.

## Loop layout

| Facet | Value |
|---|---|
| Where the loop sits | middle core (prelude-core-coda) |
| Weight sharing | fully tied |
| Passes in training | fixed |
| Passes at test time | fixed |
| Input injection | none |
| KV cache | per-pass KV |
| Gradient through passes | full BPTT |
| Origin | trained from scratch |
| FFN | MoE |
| Attention in the loop | full attention |
| Passes (L4-9) | train 2; test 2 |
| Backprop (L4-9) | both passes |

Shown for the 200M scale (L = 12) used in all design ablations; the middle 6 of 12 layers run twice, so 18 layers execute per token. All four scales loop the middle 50% twice and place ⌊(L − m)/2⌋ layers before the span (looped layers 3-7, 4-9, 6-15 and 8-22 for L = 10, 12, 20 and 30). Inside the loop each sublayer's residual update is scaled by 1/r (here 1/2), and every layer execution computes its own Q, K and V; smaller heads at a higher GQA ratio keep the KV cache close to the Baseline's.

## Results

**200M, L = 12, two passes, per-token FLOPs, total parameters and KV matched; contiguous middle span from 0 layers (Baseline) to all 12** · validation loss at S ≈ 85% / S ≈ 95% (lower is better) · Table 3

| Variant | Value |
|---|---|
| No loop (Baseline), 12 executed layers | 1.9445 / 1.8735 |
| Middle 2 layers (17%), 14 executed | 1.9384 / 1.8562 |
| Middle 4 layers (33%), 16 executed | 1.9275 / 1.8524 |
| Middle 6 layers (50%), 18 executed | 1.9257 / 1.8517 |
| Middle 8 layers (67%), 20 executed | 1.9374 / 1.8544 |
| Middle 10 layers (83%), 22 executed | 1.9413 / 1.8572 |
| All 12 layers (100%), 24 executed | 1.9322 / 1.8601 |

DCLM Core does not track validation loss in this sweep; at S ≈ 95% it peaks at 67% span (31.78) and is 29.68 at 50%. The authors select the span on validation loss and train each configuration once.

**200M, S ≈ 85%, middle 50% looped, physical depth 12, FLOPs, parameters and KV matched (more passes force a narrower model)** · validation loss / DCLM Core / DCLM Completion · Table 5

| Variant | Value |
|---|---|
| Baseline (1x), 12 executed layers | 1.9445 / 24.92 / 2.2887 |
| Looped 2x, 18 executed layers | 1.9257 / 27.57 / 2.2635 |
| Looped 3x, 24 executed layers | 1.9385 / 27.15 / 2.2779 |
| Looped 4x, 30 executed layers | 1.9360 / 27.30 / 2.2820 |

**Separate fits of L(F, S, D) for each architecture on S ≈ 85%, 95% and 97% (72 + 72 endpoints spanning 1.3x10^19 to 2.2x10^21 training FLOPs)** · CE Gain, the share of training compute SMELT saves at equal frontier loss, at S ≈ 85% / 95% / 97% · Table 7

| Variant | Value |
|---|---|
| 10^20 FLOPs | 10.0% / 7.8% / 6.8% |
| 10^21 FLOPs | 18.0% / 15.8% / 14.7% |
| 10^22 FLOPs (extrapolated) | 23.5% / 20.9% / 19.6% |

Cell-bootstrap 95% intervals are wide, e.g. [1,22] at 10^20 FLOPs and S ≈ 85%; the 10^22 row lies beyond the fitted window and two of its three intervals reach 0.

**C = 10^21 FLOPs, S ≈ 95%; per-category intercepts fitted with the aggregate exponents** · CE Gain by validation category · Section 5.2; Figure 10

| Variant | Value |
|---|---|
| Code | 20.4% |
| Finance | 16.8% |
| Math/STEM | 16.6% |
| Knowledge | 14.9% |
| Web | 14.8% |

## Other findings

- At 200M with all budgets matched, looping the middle 6 of 12 layers gives lower validation loss than looping all 12 (1.9257 vs 1.9322 at S ≈ 85%, 1.8517 vs 1.8601 at S ≈ 95%), and every span tested beats the unlooped Baseline. (Section 3.3; Table 3)
- Two passes beat three and four at matched FLOPs, parameters and KV (validation loss 1.9257 vs 1.9385 and 1.9360, DCLM Core 27.57 vs 27.15 and 27.30); the authors attribute the regression to the narrower model that extra passes force. (Section 3.5; Table 5)
- SMELT's fitted capacity and data exponents are both larger (a = 0.3892 vs 0.3703, c = 0.7011 vs 0.6594), giving frontier exponents of 0.250 vs 0.237; the irreducible losses differ by 0.005 nats, less than either fit's RMSE. (Section 4.3; Table 6)
- SMELT wins 96 of 96 matched pairs on DCLM Completion, 83 of 96 on DCLM Core and 29 of the 30 MMLU pairs whose Baseline is at least 10 points above chance, and it scores better than a Baseline at the same validation loss would (positive mean residual on all three at every scale). (Section 5.1; Figures 5-9)
- The gain is larger on longer samples and with in-context examples; the loss improvement on the four longest length buckets is 1.52x that on the four shortest, and the few-shot accuracy gap widens from 0.9 pp at k = 0 to 1.9 pp at k = 1, holding through k = 8. (Section 5.3; Figure 11)
- The second visit shrinks the attention sink; for the 1.6B Dyck head, BOS attention mass falls from 0.60 to 0.02 and mass on demonstration answers rises from 0.24 to 0.85. (Section 6.4; Figure 18)

## Comparison

- **Baseline**: Unlooped MoE Transformer from the same internal family (top-8 routing, GQA), trained on identical token sequences in each of 16 grid cells (four scales; S = 0% and S ≈ 85%, 95%, 97%).
- **Held fixed**: F (training FLOPs), N (unique parameters), KV (KV cache per token), D (training tokens)
- **Differs**: A (active parameters), L (executed layers per token)
- **Baseline hyperparameters**: shared with the looped model
- **Headline claim**: With per-token FLOPs, total non-embedding parameters and KV cache matched (typical mismatch under 4%, 1% and 4%), SMELT reaches lower loss than the Baseline at every scale and sparsity level, and its separately fitted frontier saves 6.8-18.0% of training FLOPs at 10^20-10^21 FLOPs (14.7% at 10^21 and S ≈ 97%). (Abstract; Section 1; Table 2; Table 7)

## Caveats

- Active parameters and executed depth are not matched; at 200M and S ≈ 95% SMELT has 0.142B active parameters against the Baseline's 0.209B and executes 18 layers instead of 12 (Section 3.2; Tables 9-10).
- The span, depth and loop-count ablations ran only at 200M, with one training run per configuration and the same loop count in training and evaluation; the authors note the best span or count may differ at larger scales (Section 3.3; Section 7).
- Budget matching equates arithmetic FLOPs, parameters and KV-cache size, not wall-clock cost (Section 7).
- The model family and training stack are proprietary and cannot be released, pretraining uses an internal corpus, and training contexts are 4096 tokens (Section 3.1; Appendix A).
- SMELT shares the Baseline's optimizer, schedule and data; the Baseline configurations come from a tuned MoE family, and no separate tuning for SMELT is reported (Section 3.1; Appendix A).

## Reproducibility

| Code | Weights | Configs | Data |
|---|---|---|---|
| none | none | partial | none |

## Related open questions

- [Where in the stack should the loop sit?](questions.md#loop-placement) (supports)
- [With training compute held fixed, do more passes help?](questions.md#more-passes-fixed-compute) (against)

## Authors

Shaowen Wang, Ge Zhang, Kairong Luo, Yuhao Wu, Shaofan Liu, Jiaheng Liu, Wenhao Huang, Shen Yan, Jian Li


# Parcae: Parcae: Scaling Laws For Stable Looped Language Models

English · [简体中文](../zh/2604.12946.md) · [Back to the list](../../README.md)

<sub>arXiv 2604.12946 · 2026-04-14 · University of California, San Diego, Together AI</sub>


> Constrain the loop's injection to a stable negative-diagonal form, sample depth per sequence, and fit training and test-time scaling laws for looping at fixed parameter count.

**Category**: Scaling and budget · **Status**: draft (numbers not yet re-checked) · **Impact**: cites 96 · stars 195 · HF upvotes 11

[paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.12946) · [code](https://github.com/sandyresearch/parcae) · [project](https://sandyresearch.github.io/parcae/) · [weights](https://huggingface.co/SandyResearch/parcae-140m)

## Problem

Middle-looped models such as Huginn-style RDMs diverge or show loss spikes unless hyperparameters are chosen carefully; the paper traces this to injection parameters whose linearized state matrix reaches a spectral radius of 1 or more, and asks whether a stable looped model scales predictably with loops.

## Method

- Write each loop step as h_{t+1} = Ā h_t + B̄ e + R̄(h_t, e) and parameterize A as a negative diagonal discretized with ZOH, so the spectral radius of Ā stays below 1; the prelude output e is normalized before injection.
- Sample the depth T per sequence from a Poisson distribution with mean μ_rec, backpropagate through the last μ_bwd = ⌈μ_rec/2⌉ steps, and loop the middle third of a nanochat-style Transformer.
- Fit isoFLOP scaling laws over μ_rec and tokens at fixed parameters (140M, 370M) and a saturating exponential law for loss against test-time T, then join them in one unified law.

## Loop layout

| Facet | Value |
|---|---|
| Where the loop sits | middle core (prelude-core-coda) |
| Weight sharing | fully tied |
| Passes in training | sampled |
| Passes at test time | can run more passes than trained |
| Input injection | gated |
| KV cache | n/a |
| Gradient through passes | truncated (last k passes) |
| Origin | trained from scratch |
| FFN | dense FFN |
| Attention in the loop | full attention |
| Passes (R8) | train Poisson with mean 8, per sequence; test 8 |
| Backprop (R8) | last 4 |

Shown for the 1.3B model of the Transformer comparison (Table 18), which has 8 prelude, 8 recurrent and 8 coda blocks against a 24-layer Transformer; the 140M, 370M and 770M models use 2, 4 and 6 blocks per unit, and all loop the middle third. Each step computes h_{t+1} = Ā h_t + B̄ e + R̄(h_t, e) with Ā = exp(ΔA) for a negative diagonal A (ZOH), B̄ = ΔB (Euler) and a normalized prelude output e. The Section 5.1 models are also evaluated at T = 1-16 and the Section 5.3 models up to T = 24.

## Results

**Transformer setup (simplified nanochat), FineWeb-Edu, 2,048 context, parameter- and data-matched pairs trained on 11.2B, 29.6B, 61.6B and 104B tokens at 140M, 370M, 770M and 1.3B; Parcae evaluated at T=8** · validation PPL / Core / Core-Extended · Table 5; Table 21

| Variant | Value |
|---|---|
| 140M Transformer | 21.48 / 13.00 / 8.80 |
| 140M Parcae | 19.06 / 14.04 / 9.67 |
| 370M Transformer | 15.79 / 17.46 / 11.71 |
| 370M Parcae | 14.49 / 20.00 / 12.75 |
| 770M Transformer | 13.08 / 22.42 / 14.20 |
| 770M Parcae | 12.49 / 25.07 / 15.19 |
| 1.3B Transformer | 11.95 / 25.45 / 15.90 |
| 1.3B Parcae | 11.42 / 28.44 / 17.08 |

**RDM setup of Geiping et al. (Huginn data and tokenizer); 100M evaluated at T=16, 350M at T=8** · validation PPL / WikiText PPL / zero-shot average of six tasks · Table 3

| Variant | Value |
|---|---|
| 100M RDM | 14.23 / 63.27 / 45.03 |
| 100M Parcae | 13.59 / 60.33 / 46.83 |
| 350M RDM | 10.76 / 41.31 / 49.45 |
| 350M Parcae | 10.09 / 37.53 / 50.12 |

**Transformer setup at 140M and 370M with parameters and training FLOPs fixed (tokens shrink as μ_rec grows); fixed depth means μ_rec = 1** · optimal μ_rec* / Core at μ_rec* / Core at fixed depth · Table 6; Appendix O

| Variant | Value |
|---|---|
| 140M, 1x10^18 FLOPs | 2 / 7.6 / 7.9 |
| 140M, 2x10^18 FLOPs | 2 / 9.0 / 10.5 |
| 140M, 4x10^18 FLOPs | 4 / 11.2 / 10.7 |
| 140M, 8x10^18 FLOPs | 6 / 10.5 / 11.8 |
| 140M, 16x10^18 FLOPs | 8 / 14.6 / 13.0 |
| 140M, 64x10^18 FLOPs | 10 / 16.2 / 15.0 |
| 370M, 32x10^18 FLOPs | 4 / 15.2 / 16.8 |

| 370M, 128x10^18 FLOPs | 6 / 20.1 / 18.1 |

**RDM-setup Parcae models (100M trained with μ_rec 16, 350M with μ_rec 8), depth sampled per micro-batch or per sequence** · validation PPL at test-time T = 1 / 4 / 8 / 16 · Table 8; Table 17

| Variant | Value |
|---|---|
| 100M, per-batch | 300.32 / 36.75 / 16.65 / 13.81 |
| 100M, per-sequence | 70.47 / 17.15 / 14.08 / 13.59 |
| 350M, per-batch | 167.61 / 12.80 / 10.40 / 10.24 |
| 350M, per-sequence | 17.92 / 10.49 / 10.09 / 10.11 |

## Other findings

- Run at up to twice the training mean (μ_rec = 8), the 140M-1.3B models' gains plateau near T = μ_rec; the authors read this as training depth setting the test-time ceiling. (Section 5.3; Figure 7)
- Loss against test-time T follows L(T) = L∞ + Z·exp(−zT); fitted on T ≤ μ_rec and tested on T > μ_rec, this form has the lowest error of the four forms tried (Huber loss 3.18 and 2.29 x10^-7 at 140M and 370M). (Section 5.3; Appendix L; Table 12)
- Sampling the total depth from Λ(μ_rec) and then truncating backprop, instead of sampling only the no-gradient steps as Geiping et al. do, keeps validation loss at T = 4, 16 and 64 closer to full backprop (100M models, 10B tokens, μ_rec = μ_bwd = 8). (Section 4.2; Appendix H; Figure 14)
- With parameters and FLOPs fixed, the optimal μ_rec grows with the budget (2 at 1x10^18 to 10 at 64x10^18 FLOPs for 140M) and follows a power law with exponent about 0.40; the optimal token count follows one with exponent about 0.78. (Section 5.2; Table 6; Figure 5)
- In early RDM runs made before the Appendix H sampling fix (10B tokens, μ_bwd = 4, evaluated at T = μ_rec), μ_rec = 8 gave the lowest validation loss (2.453) among values from 4 to 32; in a second sweep at μ_rec = 20 (8.5B tokens), raising μ_bwd from 4 to 12 lowered it from 2.500 to 2.474. (Appendix I; Table 9; Table 10)
- Across learning rates from 2e-4 to 1e-3, the Pre-Norm RDM converges only at 2e-4 and the residual-norm RDM up to 4e-4, while Parcae converges at all five. (Table 2; Appendix F)

## Comparison

- **Baseline**: Fixed-depth Transformers in a simplified nanochat setup with the same parameter count and training data; Huginn-style RDMs with matched parameters and data are a second baseline.
- **Held fixed**: N (unique parameters), D (training tokens)
- **Differs**: F (training FLOPs), L (executed layers per token)
- **Baseline hyperparameters**: tuned separately
- **Headline claim**: At 1.3B parameters and the same data, Parcae (T=8) scores 28.44 Core and 17.08 Core-Extended against the Transformer's 25.45 and 15.90 (+2.99 and +1.18 points); the 770M Parcae's 25.07 Core is comparable to the 1.3B Transformer with roughly half the parameters. (Abstract; Section 5.1; Table 5)

## Caveats

- Experiments stop at 1.3B parameters, 104B tokens and a 2,048-token context with dense FFNs; the scaling laws are fitted only at 140M and 370M, and the authors say their observations are limited to small architectures (Section 6).
- Parameters and data are matched (Parcae has 0.35-0.83% more parameters, Table 19) but compute is not; at T = 8 the recurrent block runs 8 times per token, and the paper reports neither KV-cache size nor inference cost.
- The Transformer and RDM baselines got their own learning-rate sweeps, and Parcae reused the baselines' best settings without a sweep of its own (Section 5.1; Appendix Q).
- Test-time gains saturate near the training mean μ_rec, and the authors note that a larger μ_rec needs more test-time steps for equivalent quality (Section 5.3; Section 6).

## Reproducibility

| Code | Weights | Configs | Data |
|---|---|---|---|
| available | available | available | available |

## Open weights

- Parcae: [SandyResearch/parcae-140m](https://huggingface.co/SandyResearch/parcae-140m), [SandyResearch/parcae-370m](https://huggingface.co/SandyResearch/parcae-370m), [SandyResearch/parcae-770m](https://huggingface.co/SandyResearch/parcae-770m), [SandyResearch/parcae-1.3b](https://huggingface.co/SandyResearch/parcae-1.3b)

## Related open questions

- [Does running more passes at test time than in training keep improving quality?](questions.md#extra-passes-at-test-time) (partly)
- [With training compute held fixed, do more passes help?](questions.md#more-passes-fixed-compute) (partly)

## Authors

Hayden Prairie, Zachary Novack, Taylor Berg-Kirkpatrick, Daniel Y. Fu


# YOCO-U: Universal YOCO for Efficient Depth Scaling

English · [简体中文](../zh/2604.01220.md) · [Back to the list](../../README.md)

<sub>arXiv 2604.01220 · 2026-04-01 · Microsoft Research, Tsinghua University</sub>


> Loop only YOCO's self-decoder, whose layers use sliding-window attention, so extra depth costs compute while the cross-decoder's global KV is still computed once.

**Category**: Architecture: where to loop, what to share · **Status**: draft (numbers not yet re-checked) · **Impact**: cites 4 · HF upvotes 18

[paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.01220)

## Problem

Looping a standard Transformer re-runs every layer, which regenerates KV caches and repeats global attention, so memory and compute grow with depth.

## Method

- Start from YOCO, where an L/2-layer self-decoder with efficient self-attention (SWA by default) produces one global KV cache that every layer of the L/2-layer cross-decoder reads through cross-attention.
- Replace the self-decoder with a Universal Self-Decoder that applies the same L/2 layers T times in sequence (T=3 by default, 2× the total FLOPs of the non-recursive baseline).
- Project the global KV from the final iteration's output, so its size does not depend on T; only the SWA window caches grow with T.

## Loop layout

| Facet | Value |
|---|---|
| Where the loop sits | KV-producing half (CED encoder / YOCO self-decoder) |
| Weight sharing | fully tied |
| Passes in training | fixed |
| Passes at test time | fixed |
| Input injection | none |
| KV cache | one global KV per token |
| Gradient through passes | n/a |
| Origin | trained from scratch |
| FFN | MoE |
| Attention in the loop | hybrid (full + window / linear) |
| Passes (Universal Self-Decoder, SWA-512) | train 3; test 3 |

Section 4.1 model, a 20-layer YOCO with MoE FFNs (1.3B activated, 10B total). The 10-layer self-decoder uses SWA with window 512 and RoPE and is applied T=3 times with shared weights; its final output is projected once into the global KV that all 10 cross-decoder layers (NoPE) read. Each iteration keeps its own window cache. Figure 6 trains separate 1.3B models with 1, 2, 3 and 5 loops.

## Results

**Section 4.1 MoE (1.3B activated, 10B total), 20 layers, 8192 training length, trained up to 300B tokens, T=3** · MMLU / GSM8K / Average (LM Eval-Harness) · Table 2; Section 4.1

| Variant | Value |
|---|---|
| YOCO | 49.59 / 38.06 / 41.78 |
| YOCO-U (Equal FLOPS) | 54.63 / 50.49 / 46.23 |
| YOCO-U (Equal Steps) | 55.63 / 50.57 / 47.08 |

The paper does not state how many training tokens the Equal FLOPS row used.

**Thinking SFT from the 280B checkpoint, 20B tokens of math thinking data, 32768 maximal length; greedy decoding up to 32,768 tokens** · average accuracy over 11 math benchmarks (%) · Figure 3; Section 4.1; Appendix B

| Variant | Value |
|---|---|
| YOCO | 42.7 |
| YOCO-U | 67.1 |

**1.3B dense, 20 layers, hidden 2560, 20B tokens; the compute-scaling variants are aligned to approximately 2× the FLOPs of a standard 20-layer Transformer** · WikiText ppl / Avg. accuracy · Table 3; Appendix E

| Variant | Value |
|---|---|
| Transformer | 22.52 / 47.1 |
| YOCO | 22.25 / 47.0 |
| Loop/Universal TRM (whole model looped 2 times) | 21.56 / 47.8 |
| ParScale | 23.13 / 46.8 |
| RINS (early-layer recursion) | 20.98 / 48.3 |
| YOCO-U | 21.01 / 48.3 |

**1.3B dense ablations; the YOCO and YOCO-U rows repeat the Table 3 values at two decimals** · WikiText ppl / Avg. accuracy · Table 5; Section 4.3

| Variant | Value |
|---|---|
| YOCO | 22.25 / 46.95 |
| Deep (Instead of Wide) | 22.04 / 46.87 |
| YOCO-U | 21.01 / 48.25 |
| Deeper (Instead of Wide) | 21.42 / 48.59 |
| Upper Loop (Cross-Decoder) | 22.15 / 47.34 |
| Upper Loop w/o Shared KV | 22.06 / 46.41 |

Deep and Deeper double the depth at the same model size (Deeper has hidden size 1792 and 40 layers). Upper Loop loops the cross-decoder instead of the self-decoder; the w/o Shared KV variant uses self-attention there.

**1.3B configuration of Section 4.4, Nano-vLLM in BF16 on H100-80GB, generation batch size 32, length 128** · at 256K length, prefill tokens/s / decode tokens/s / KV cache MB · Tables 8-10; Appendix D

| Variant | Value |
|---|---|
| Transformer | 7475 / 137 / 10240 |
| YOCO | 220407 / 318 / 522 |
| RINS | 3739 / 56 / 20480 |
| YOCO-U | 76301 / 303 / 542 |

Section 4.5 states that YOCO-U gives up 5% of YOCO's decoding throughput, decodes 2.21× faster than the Transformer at 256K, and that RINS needs 38× the KV memory of YOCO-U.

## Other findings

- Looping the cross-decoder instead of the self-decoder averages 47.34 (46.41 without the shared KV), against 48.25 for YOCO-U and 46.95 for non-recursive YOCO; the authors conclude that recursion on deeper layers gives diminishing improvement regardless of the KV cache strategy. (Table 5; Section 4.3)
- At about 2× FLOPs, looping the whole 20-layer Transformer twice averages 47.8, while RINS and YOCO-U both reach 48.3; the authors read this as scaling FLOPs on bottom blocks being more effective than on all blocks. (Table 3; Section 4.2; Appendix E)
- Separately trained 1.3B models with 1, 2, 3 and 5 loops show consistent improvements in validation loss as the loop count grows; Loop=5 uses 3 times the FLOPs of the non-recursive model. The figure prints no per-loop values. (Figure 6; Section 4.4)
- YOCO-U trained on 80B tokens is comparable with non-recursive YOCO trained on 210B tokens (approximately 62% fewer tokens). (Figure 2; Section 4.1)
- With training steps fixed, YOCO-U matches YOCO with 50% fewer parameters; when activated parameters are aligned, the authors say YOCO-U narrows the gap to non-recursive models and is near-comparable above 10B. (Figure 5; Section 4.4)
- On Needle-in-a-Haystack, YOCO-U scores 1.00 (S-NIAH-1) and 0.95 (S-NIAH-2), against 0.87 and 0.82 for the Transformer and 0.99 and 0.91 for RINS. (Table 4)

## Comparison

- **Baseline**: Non-recursive YOCO with the same configuration and hyperparameters (Loop=1); Section 4.2 adds a Transformer, a Universal Transformer looped twice, RINS and ParScale at 1.3B dense.
- **Held fixed**: N (unique parameters), A (active parameters), F (training FLOPs)
- **Differs**: D (training tokens), L (executed layers per token), KV (KV cache per token)
- **Baseline hyperparameters**: shared with the looped model
- **Headline claim**: With the same 1.3B-activated / 10B-total MoE, YOCO-U at equal training FLOPs averages 46.23 on the Table 2 tasks against 41.78 for non-recursive YOCO (+4.45), and 47.08 at equal steps; at equal FLOPs its loss is lower by 0.033. (Section 4.1; Table 2; Figure 2)

## Caveats

- The headline runs are a 1.3B-activated / 10B-total MoE trained on up to 300B tokens; the architecture comparison, ablations and loop scaling use 1.3B dense models trained on 20B tokens, and the efficiency tests use the same 1.3B configuration. Training length is 8192 in Sections 4.1 and 4.4.
- Each model is trained and tested with one fixed loop count (3 by default; 1, 2, 3 and 5 in Figure 6); the paper does not report changing the loop count at inference.
- Training FLOPs are computed as tokens × layers (Section 4.1), and the Equal FLOPS row of Table 2 does not state its token count.
- The KV cache is not identical to YOCO's because each self-decoder iteration keeps its own window cache (Table 10, 46 MB vs 26 MB at 8K and 542 vs 522 MB at 256K).
- Prefill throughput is below non-recursive YOCO's, 76301 vs 220407 tokens/s at 256K (Table 8).
- Table 5 does not state the loop count or FLOPs of the Upper Loop variants.

## Reproducibility

|---|---|---|---|
| none | none | partial | none |

- [Can later passes reuse one KV cache instead of keeping KV for every pass?](questions.md#shared-kv-across-passes) (supports)

## Authors

Yutao Sun, Li Dong, Tianzhu Ye, Shaohan Huang, Jianyong Wang, Furu Wei


# Retrofitted Recurrence: Teaching Pretrained Language Models to Think Deeper with Retrofitted Recurrence

English · [简体中文](../zh/2511.07384.md) · [Back to the list](../../README.md)

<sub>arXiv 2511.07384 · 2025-11-10 · University of Maryland, New York University, Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory, University of North Carolina, ELLIS Institute Tübingen, Max Planck Institute for Intelligent Systems, Tübingen AI Center, Columbia University</sub>


> Turn pretrained 1B models into prelude-core-coda recurrent models by dropping middle layers and looping a block, then keep training while a curriculum raises the mean recurrence.

**Category**: Training and retrofitting · **Status**: draft (numbers not yet re-checked) · **Impact**: cites 83 · stars 73 · HF upvotes 21

[paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2511.07384) · [code](https://github.com/mcleish7/retrofitting-recurrence) · [weights](https://huggingface.co/collections/tomg-group-umd/retrofitting-recurrence)

## Problem

Pretraining a depth-recurrent model from scratch is costly. Huginn-0125 used 800B tokens, and running many recurrences per step slows training compared with a fixed-depth model of the same parameter count. The paper studies how to convert existing pretrained non-recurrent models into recurrent ones efficiently.

## Method

- Take a pretrained model's early layers as the prelude and later layers as the recurrent core and coda, dropping the layers in between, e.g. (4,8,4) from TinyLlama-1.1B-3T and (4,6,4) from OLMo-2-0425-1B and Llama-3.2-1B.
- Keep Huginn-0125's recurrence, with a linear adapter on concat(prelude output, state), a random initial state, a Poisson-Lognormal recurrence count and gradients through at most the last 8 core passes.
- Raise the mean of the recurrence distribution with a curriculum (1-sqrt over the first 75% of training in the main runs) to 4, 8, 16 or 32, and optimize with Muon.
- Train on about 50B tokens of Nemotron-CC-Math-v1-4plus. To keep general ability, first heal on 26B tokens of FineWeb-Edu, then train on 26B tokens mixing FineWeb-Edu with Nemotron SFT data.

## Loop layout

| Facet | Value |
|---|---|
| Where the loop sits | middle core (prelude-core-coda) |
| Weight sharing | fully tied |
| Passes in training | scheduled curriculum |
| Passes at test time | can run more passes than trained |
| Input injection | concat + projection |
| KV cache | n/a |
| Gradient through passes | truncated (last k passes) |
| Origin | retrofitted from a pretrained model |
| FFN | dense FFN |
| Attention in the loop | full attention |
| Passes (L10-17) | train Poisson-Lognormal, mean ramped to 4, 8, 16 or 32; test 1-32 |
| Backprop (L10-17) | last 8 |

Shown is TinyLlama (4,8,4); labels are layer indices in the 22-layer TinyLlama-1.1B-3T parent, whose layers 4-9 are dropped. OLMo-2-0425-1B and Llama-3.2-1B use (4,6,4) with layers L0-3, L6-11 and L12-15, dropping L4-5. Sections 4.1-4.2 use a (2,4,2) model built from Llama-3.2-1B. The recurrence count is sampled from a Poisson-Lognormal distribution whose mean follows the curriculum, so depth is both sampled and scheduled.

## Results

**TinyLlama-1.1B-3T converted to (4,8,4), about 50B tokens of Nemotron-CC-Math-v1-4plus, test recurrence 32** · GSM8K | MATH accuracy (1-shot) · Table 3

| Variant | Value |
|---|---|
| Non-recurrent TinyLlama, same data | 26.6 \| 24.0 |
| Train recurrence 4 | 37.9 \| 26.0 |
| Train recurrence 8 | 41.0 \| 25.9 |
| Train recurrence 16 | 43.7 \| 29.0 |
| Train recurrence 32 | 45.0 \| 27.1 |

**OLMo-2-0425-1B converted to (4,6,4), same data, test recurrence 32** · GSM8K | MATH accuracy (1-shot) · Table 4

| Variant | Value |
|---|---|
| Non-recurrent OLMo, same data | 35.3 \| 25.1 |
| Train recurrence 4 | 40.6 \| 27.6 |
| Train recurrence 8 | 44.6 \| 28.1 |
| Train recurrence 16 | 48.3 \| 29.0 |
| Train recurrence 32 | 51.6 \| 29.3 |

**Llama-3.2-1B converted to (4,6,4), same data, test recurrence 32** · GSM8K | MATH accuracy (1-shot) · Table 5

| Variant | Value |
|---|---|
| Non-recurrent Llama, same data | 37.1 \| 27.4 |
| Train recurrence 4 | 40.0 \| 28.9 |
| Train recurrence 8 | 44.7 \| 29.6 |
| Train recurrence 16 | 45.3 \| 28.4 |
| Train recurrence 32 | 49.4 \| 31.5 |

**TinyLlama (4,8,4) at train recurrence 4. Single phase is 26B tokens of FineWeb-Edu mixed with Nemotron SFT data; two phase first trains on 26B tokens of FineWeb-Edu (52B in total)** · Arc-C | MMLU | GSM8K · Table 1

| Variant | Value |
|---|---|
| Recurrent, two phase, test recurrence 1 | 31.6 \| 36.2 \| 26.5 |
| Recurrent, two phase, test recurrence 32 | 37.7 \| 44.8 \| 51.2 |
| Recurrent, single phase, test recurrence 32 | 32.7 \| 39.4 \| 52.0 |
| Non-recurrent, two phase | 36.5 \| 44.4 \| 45.2 |
| Non-recurrent, single phase | 35.2 \| 45.1 \| 46.2 |

**(2,4,2) model, about 120B tokens of FineWeb-Edu, mean recurrence 32, zero-shot** · Arc-C | HellaSwag · Table 2 (Appendix C.1)

| Variant | Value |
|---|---|
| Random (Takase) init, test recurrence 1 | 23.4 \| 28.6 |
| Random (Takase) init, test recurrence 32 | 29.5 \| 48.3 |
| Llama-3.2-1B init, test recurrence 1 | 23.8 \| 34.8 |
| Llama-3.2-1B init, test recurrence 32 | 35.0 \| 55.6 |

## Other findings

- Linearly ramping the mean recurrence up to 32 slightly lowers validation loss per step and greatly lowers it per training FLOP ((2,4,2) from Llama, 48 hours on 4 MI300A GPUs, about 1e20 FLOPs). (Section 4.2; Figure 3)
- On GSM8K, larger training recurrences give a larger gain per training FLOP for OLMo and Llama, but not for TinyLlama. (Section 4.3.2; Figure 20)
- A 26B-token FineWeb-Edu healing phase before the mixed data raises the recurrent model's Arc-C by 5% over single-phase training, while the non-recurrent model changes little. (Section 4.4; Figure 8)
- Among the tested layer choices for a (2,4,2) model from Llama-1b, taking early layers for the prelude and later layers for the core and coda gave the lowest training loss; on TinyLlama (4,8,4) this choice also reached lower loss than layers picked with ShortGPT. (Appendix C.1.1; Figures 12 and 13)
- Muon trains the recurrent models more stably than AdamW, whose loss spiked to NaN at learning rate 5e-5; for the non-recurrent TinyLlama the gap is much smaller, with a small gain for Muon. (Section 4.3.1; Figure 4)

## Comparison

- **Baseline**: The parent model (TinyLlama, OLMo or Llama) post-trained without recurrence on the same data in the same order. Figures 5-7 compare accuracy against training FLOPs and at the final checkpoint.
- **Held fixed**: D (training tokens)
- **Differs**: N (unique parameters), F (training FLOPs), L (executed layers per token)
- **Baseline hyperparameters**: shared with the looped model
- **Headline claim**: Converting a pretrained model to a recurrent one gives better math accuracy at a given training compute budget than post-training the non-recurrent model. After the same ~50B math tokens, OLMo (4,6,4) at train and test recurrence 32 scores 51.6 on GSM8K and 29.3 on MATH, against 35.3 and 25.1 for the post-trained non-recurrent OLMo. (Abstract; Section 4.3; Table 4)

## Caveats

- Models have about 1B parameters and are post-trained on about 50B tokens (about 120B in the initialization study); the authors say larger model and data scales still need testing.
- All models are trained with a 1024-token context.
- Against the non-recurrent parent, data and tokens are matched but parameters and compute are not. The recurrent models keep 72.7% (TinyLlama) or 87.5% (OLMo, Llama) of the parent's parameters and use more FLOPs per training step.
- All models share one hyperparameter set (Muon with learning rate 0.001 and weight decay 1e-4, Appendix D); the baselines are not tuned separately.
- Training only on math slightly lowers HellaSwag, Arc and OpenBookQA (Section 4.4). GSM8K and MATH use one in-context example, flexible extract for GSM8K and Minerva criteria with Math-Verify for MATH.

## Reproducibility

|---|---|---|---|
| available | available | available | partial |

## Open weights

- Recurrent-Llama-3.2 (4,6,4): [smcleish/Recurrent-Llama-3.2-train-recurrence-4](https://huggingface.co/smcleish/Recurrent-Llama-3.2-train-recurrence-4), [smcleish/Recurrent-Llama-3.2-train-recurrence-8](https://huggingface.co/smcleish/Recurrent-Llama-3.2-train-recurrence-8), [smcleish/Recurrent-Llama-3.2-train-recurrence-16](https://huggingface.co/smcleish/Recurrent-Llama-3.2-train-recurrence-16), [smcleish/Recurrent-Llama-3.2-train-recurrence-32](https://huggingface.co/smcleish/Recurrent-Llama-3.2-train-recurrence-32), [smcleish/Recurrent-Llama-3.2-untrained](https://huggingface.co/smcleish/Recurrent-Llama-3.2-untrained)
- Recurrent-OLMo-2-0425 (4,6,4): [smcleish/Recurrent-OLMo-2-0425-train-recurrence-4](https://huggingface.co/smcleish/Recurrent-OLMo-2-0425-train-recurrence-4), [smcleish/Recurrent-OLMo-2-0425-train-recurrence-8](https://huggingface.co/smcleish/Recurrent-OLMo-2-0425-train-recurrence-8), [smcleish/Recurrent-OLMo-2-0425-train-recurrence-16](https://huggingface.co/smcleish/Recurrent-OLMo-2-0425-train-recurrence-16), [smcleish/Recurrent-OLMo-2-0425-train-recurrence-32](https://huggingface.co/smcleish/Recurrent-OLMo-2-0425-train-recurrence-32), [smcleish/Recurrent-OLMo-2-0425-untrained](https://huggingface.co/smcleish/Recurrent-OLMo-2-0425-untrained)
- Recurrent-TinyLlama-3T (4,8,4): [smcleish/Recurrent-TinyLlama-3T-train-recurrence-4](https://huggingface.co/smcleish/Recurrent-TinyLlama-3T-train-recurrence-4), [smcleish/Recurrent-TinyLlama-3T-train-recurrence-8](https://huggingface.co/smcleish/Recurrent-TinyLlama-3T-train-recurrence-8), [smcleish/Recurrent-TinyLlama-3T-train-recurrence-16](https://huggingface.co/smcleish/Recurrent-TinyLlama-3T-train-recurrence-16), [smcleish/Recurrent-TinyLlama-3T-train-recurrence-32](https://huggingface.co/smcleish/Recurrent-TinyLlama-3T-train-recurrence-32), [smcleish/Recurrent-TinyLlama-3T-train-recurrence-4-single-phase](https://huggingface.co/smcleish/Recurrent-TinyLlama-3T-train-recurrence-4-single-phase), [smcleish/Recurrent-TinyLlama-3T-train-recurrence-4-two-phase](https://huggingface.co/smcleish/Recurrent-TinyLlama-3T-train-recurrence-4-two-phase), [smcleish/Recurrent-TinyLlama-3T-untrained](https://huggingface.co/smcleish/Recurrent-TinyLlama-3T-untrained)

## Authors

Sean McLeish, Ang Li, John Kirchenbauer, Dayal Singh Kalra, Brian R. Bartoldson, Bhavya Kailkhura, Avi Schwarzschild, Jonas Geiping, Tom Goldstein, Micah Goldblum


# Ouro (LoopLM): Scaling Latent Reasoning via Looped Language Models

English · [简体中文](../zh/2510.25741.md) · [Back to the list](../../README.md)

<sub>arXiv 2510.25741 · 2025-10-29 · ByteDance Seed, UC Santa Cruz, Princeton University, Mila - Quebec AI Institute, University of Montreal, Peking University, Carnegie Mellon University, University of Pennsylvania, Conscium, University of Manchester, M-A-P</sub>


> Pre-train a weight-tied layer stack that repeats 4 times, with a learned exit gate, on 7.7T tokens; the authors report that the 1.4B and 2.6B models match dense models of up to 12B parameters.

**Category**: Depth control · **Status**: draft (numbers not yet re-checked) · **Impact**: cites 267 · HF upvotes 146 · HN points 84

[paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.25741) · [project](https://ouro-llm.github.io) · [weights](https://huggingface.co/ByteDance/Ouro-1.4B)

## Problem

LLMs mostly learn to reason through explicit chain-of-thought added after pre-training. The paper asks whether looping shared layers in latent space, built into pre-training at multi-trillion-token scale, scales better than non-recursive Transformers.

## Method

- Repeat the whole decoder stack (24 layers for 1.4B, 48 for 2.6B) with shared weights; after every step an LM head computes a loss and an exit gate predicts the probability of stopping.
- Stage I minimizes the per-step losses weighted by the gate's exit distribution minus an entropy bonus, which equals a KL term toward a uniform prior over exit steps up to a constant.
- Stage II freezes the LM and trains only the gate to continue while the next step still lowers the loss by more than a threshold; at inference the model exits at the first step whose cumulative exit probability reaches q.
- Pre-train on 7.7T tokens in four stages (8 steps in Stage 1a, then 4; the 2.6B model is upcycled from the 24-layer model), then run reasoning SFT on about 8.3M examples for the Thinking models.

## Loop layout

| Facet | Value |
|---|---|
| Where the loop sits | whole stack |
| Weight sharing | fully tied |
| Passes in training | learned / adaptive |
| Passes at test time | adaptive exit / routing |
| Input injection | none |
| KV cache | per-pass KV |
| Gradient through passes | full BPTT |
| Origin | trained from scratch |
| FFN | dense FFN |
| Attention in the loop | full attention |
| Passes (whole stack (2.6B: 48 layers)) | train 8 in Stage 1a, then 4; test 4 by default; the exit gate can stop earlier |

The whole decoder stack loops: Ouro 1.4B repeats its 24 layers and Ouro 2.6B its 48 layers, which were upcycled from the 24 layers by layer duplication; embedding and LM head sit outside the loop. The embedding enters only before the first step, and each step takes the previous step's output. After every step an LM head and an exit gate read the hidden state. Training always runs T_max steps and weights each step's loss by the learned exit distribution. Each step keeps its own KV cache.

## Results

**Base models; Ouro runs 4 recurrent steps (R4); all models use the same evaluation pipeline (Appendix C.1)** · MMLU / MMLU-Pro / BBH / GSM8K / MATH500 · Table 7

|---|---|
| Ouro 1.4B R4 (1.4B params, 7.7T tokens) | 67.35 / 48.62 / 71.02 / 78.92 / 82.40 |
| Qwen3 1.7B (1.7B, 36T) | 62.46 / 37.27 / 53.51 / 70.28 / 25.80 |
| Gemma3 4B (4.0B, 4T) | 58.37 / 34.61 / 66.32 / 68.69 / 68.60 |
| Qwen3 4B (4.0B, 36T) | 73.19 / 51.40 / 70.95 / 72.86 / 59.60 |

Each setting reports the best of 3 random seeds (Appendix B.2).

## Other findings

- Training with 8 recurrent steps in Stage 1a led to loss spikes and gradient oscillations, so the authors cut to 4 steps from Stage 1b on. (Section 4.3)
- The trained depth is not always best for the Thinking models. The 1.4B model scores higher at T=5 than at T=4 on OlympiadBench (72.30 vs 71.55) and SuperGPQA (48.73 vs 47.37), and the 2.6B model peaks at T=3 on AIME 2024 (70.33, against 64.70 at T=4). (Tables 12-13)
- Safety on HEx-PHI improves as the number of recurrent steps grows (tested 1-8), including the extrapolated steps 5-8. At 4 steps the harmful rate is 0.009 for Ouro 1.4B Thinking and 0.003 for Ouro 2.6B Thinking (Qwen3-4B-Thinking 0.009). (Section 7.1; Figure 8a)
- On MMLU, the gate with Stage II exit training reaches 66% accuracy at an average of 2.5 exit rounds, against about 64% for the gate from pre-training alone; fixed-depth exit gives 40% at 1 round and 67.35% at 4. (Section 5.4.1; Figure 5)
- Reusing KV caches during prefill costs more than 10 points on GSM8K, so all four steps keep their own KV during prefill. (Section 5.4.2)
- On the synthetic Capo task, looped (4 steps) and non-looped models with the same parameter count both store about 2 bits of knowledge per parameter. (Section 6.1; Figure 6 (left))
- In 20B-token FineWeb-Edu runs at 53M-1.36B, a Standard model with unshared layers and the same executed depth scores higher than LoopLM in every case, and the gap grows with the step count (in Table 18 the 1.3B gap is 0.017 at 2 steps and 0.025 at 4). (Appendix D.1; Table 18)

## Comparison

- **Baseline**: Public dense base models run through the same evaluation pipeline (Gemma3, Llama3.1/3.2, Qwen2.5 and Qwen3, 1B to 12B); the Thinking models are compared with Qwen3 and DeepSeek-Distill-Qwen.
- **Held fixed**: none
- **Differs**: N (unique parameters), D (training tokens)
- **Baseline hyperparameters**: not stated
- **Headline claim**: Ouro 1.4B R4 (7.7T tokens) matches or beats the 4B Qwen3-Base (36T tokens) on BBH (71.02 vs 70.95), GSM8K (78.92 vs 72.86) and MATH500 (82.40 vs 59.60); Ouro 2.6B R4 scores 55.73 on MMLU-Pro, 80.46 on BBH and 90.85 on MATH500, against 53.72, 77.65 and 62.30 for the 8B Qwen3-Base. (Section 5.1; Tables 7-8)

## Caveats

- The headline comparisons (Tables 7-9) are against separately trained public models that differ in parameters and training tokens (2T-36T); no budget is matched, and Ouro runs its stack 4 times per token.
- The models are trained at 4 steps; base benchmark scores are strongest around T=4 and degrade moderately at T=5-8, and the Thinking models degrade at T=6-8 (Tables 10-13).
- By default every step keeps its own KV cache (4× memory at 4 steps); last-step-only reuse was tested for decoding only, because prefill needs all four caches (Section 5.4.2).
- Reasoning results come from an in-house harness with an LLM judge and temperature 1.0, top_p 0.7 for every model (Section 5.2; Table 17).
- Controlled looped-versus-unlooped studies are small; they use synthetic tasks (Capo with 1M-40M GPT-2-style models, Mano, multi-hop QA) and 53M-1.36B models trained on 20B FineWeb-Edu tokens (Section 6; Appendix D).
- The authors did not run exhaustive learning-rate sweeps (Section 4.3), and RLVR with DAPO and GRPO did not improve on the SFT checkpoint (Section 4.5).
