# PLT: Parallel Loop Transformer for Efficient Test-Time Computation Scaling

English · [简体中文](../zh/2510.24824.md) · [Back to the list](../../README.md)

<sub>arXiv 2510.24824 · 2025-10-28 · ByteDance Seed</sub>


> Run loop l of token i in the same forward pass as loop l+1 of token i-1, let later loops reuse the first loop's KV plus a gated SWA, and a looped model decodes at close to unlooped latency and KV.

**Category**: Systems and inference · **Status**: draft (numbers not yet re-checked) · **Impact**: cites 38 · HF upvotes 18 · HN points 3

[paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.24824)

## Problem

In a vanilla looped Transformer the loops run one after another, so per-token compute, decoding latency and KV cache all grow linearly with the number of loops.

## Method

- Cross-loop parallelism (CLP) shifts the previous loop's last-layer states right by one token and adds the embeddings before each non-first loop, so loop l of token i, loop l+1 of token i-1 and so on are decoded as one micro-batch in a single forward pass.
- Non-first loops keep their own queries but attend globally to the first loop's KV, so only one global KV cache is stored.
- Gated SWA (G-SWA) lets non-first loops also attend to their own KV within a 64-token window and mixes local and global outputs through a head-wise sigmoid gate; these loops cache only the most recent w KV entries.

## Loop layout

| Facet | Value |
|---|---|
| Where the loop sits | shifted / parallel across tokens |
| Weight sharing | fully tied |
| Passes in training | fixed |
| Passes at test time | fixed |
| Input injection | additive |
| KV cache | first-pass KV shared |
| Gradient through passes | n/a |
| Origin | trained from scratch |
| FFN | MoE |
| Attention in the loop | hybrid (full + window / linear) |
| Passes (all layers, every loop) | train 2 or 3 (PLT-2 / PLT-3); test 2 or 3, same as training |

Each loop runs the whole stack with tied weights. Before every non-first loop, the previous loop's last-layer states are shifted right by one token and added to the token embeddings, so at decoding time loop l of token i runs in the same forward pass as loop l+1 of token i-1. Non-first loops attend globally to the first loop's KV and locally to their own KV through SWA (w=64), mixed by a head-wise sigmoid gate. The in-house Seed-MoE layer count is not disclosed; the open-source OLMo/OLMoE runs use 16 layers (Appendix A.2.1).

## Results

**In-house Seed-MoE, 680M activated / 13B total, 150B tokens; latency and KV cache at batch size 4** · Avg. accuracy / decoding latency (ms) / KV cache · Table 2

| Variant | Value |
|---|---|
| (1)Seed-MoE 680M/13B | 34.7 / 4.8 / 280M |
| (2)+loop-2 | 39.7 / 9.4 / 560M |
| (3)+loop-2+CLP | 39.6 / 5.9 / 560M |
| (4)+loop-2+CLP+KV share | 36.2 / 4.8 / 280M |
| (5)+loop-2+CLP+KV share+G-SWA(PLT-2) | 39.7 / 4.9 / 284M |
| (6)+loop-3+CLP+KV share+G-SWA(PLT-3) | 40.8 / 5.0 / 287M |

The Section 3.1.2 text gives PLT-3's latency as 4.8→4.9 ms; Table 2 prints 5.0 ms.

**Same models as Table 2; FP8 attention, W4A8 linear layers, 5000-token prefill, one GPU, mean of five runs that each decode 256 tokens** · per-token decoding latency in ms (ratio to Seed-MoE), bs=4 / bs=64 · Table 3; Section 3.1.1

| Variant | Value |
|---|---|
| (1)Seed-MoE 680M/13B | 4.8(1.00×) / 10.9(1.00×) |
| (2)+loop-2 | 9.4(1.96×) / 21.4(1.96×) |
| (3)+loop-2+CLP | 5.9(1.23×) / 16.4(1.50×) |
| (4)+loop-2+CLP+KV share | 4.8(1.00×) / 11.1(1.02×) |
| (5)+loop-2+CLP+KV share+G-SWA(PLT-2) | 4.9(1.02×) / 11.3(1.04×) |

**In-house MoE, baseline trained on 1T tokens; PLT-2 uses two-thirds of the baseline's layers** · Avg. accuracy · Table 4; Section 3.2

| Variant | Value |
|---|---|
| Seed-MoE (2.5B/60B) | 62.1 |
| PLT-2 (1.7B/40B) | 62.6 |

Section 3.2 reports about 30% lower decoding latency for PLT-2 across batch sizes 4 to 64 (Figure 5) and a KV cache roughly two-thirds of the baseline's.

**OLMo-based 1.2B dense and OLMoE-based 1B/7B MoE, 16 layers, 400B tokens, L=2** · Loss / Avg. accuracy · Table 5; Appendix A.2.1

| Variant | Value |
|---|---|
| Vanilla Dense | 2.577 / 55.4 |
| Dense + loop-2 | 2.532 / 57.6 |
| Dense + PLT-2 | 2.537 / 57.4 |
| Vanilla MoE | 2.342 / 57.8 |
| MoE + loop-2 | 2.302 / 59.6 |
| MoE + PLT-2 | 2.280 / 60.0 |

**OLMo-based dense ablation (hidden 1536, GQA with 16 query and 4 KV heads), 100B tokens, latency on one H800** · Loss / Avg. accuracy / latency in ms at bs=1 / at bs=16 · Table 6; Appendix A.3.1

| Variant | Value |
|---|---|
| (1) Vanilla Dense | 2.880 / 46.6 / 1.68 / 2.49 |
| (2) +loop-2 | 2.856 / 46.7 / 2.66 / 3.92 |
| (3) +loop-2+CLP | 2.840 / 47.8 / 1.73 / 3.23 |
| (4) +loop-2+CLP+KVshare | 2.858 / 46.9 / 1.73 / 2.69 |
| (5) +loop-2+CLP+KVshare+G-SWA | 2.844 / 47.8 / 1.73 / 2.70 |

## Other findings

- Adding CLP to the two-loop model leaves average accuracy nearly unchanged (39.7 to 39.6) and cuts decoding latency from 9.4 ms to 5.9 ms, while the KV cache stays at 560M. (Table 2; Section 3.1.2)
- Sharing the first loop's KV halves the KV cache (560M to 280M) but lowers average accuracy from 39.6 to 36.2; adding G-SWA with a 64-token window brings it back to 39.7 at 284M. (Table 2; Section 3.1.2)
- With the same parameters, three loops beat two, with average accuracy 40.8 for PLT-3 against 39.7 for PLT-2; Table 2 lists 5.0 vs 4.9 ms latency and 287M vs 284M KV. (Table 2; Section 3.1.2)
- At batch sizes 32 and 64, PLT-2 cuts per-token decoding latency by 47% relative to the vanilla two-loop model and runs at 1.06× and 1.04× the latency of the unlooped model. (Table 3; Section 3.1.3)
- A PLT-2 with two-thirds of the baseline's layers (1.7B/40B) averages 62.6 against 62.1 for the 2.5B/60B Seed-MoE, with about 30% lower decoding latency. (Table 4; Section 3.2; Figure 5)

## Comparison

- **Baseline**: Unlooped in-house Seed-MoE 680M/13B and the same model looped twice without CLP; CLP, KV sharing and G-SWA are then added one at a time.
- **Held fixed**: N (unique parameters), A (active parameters), D (training tokens)
- **Differs**: F (training FLOPs), L (executed layers per token), KV (KV cache per token)
- **Baseline hyperparameters**: not stated
- **Headline claim**: On a 680M/13B MoE trained on 150B tokens, PLT-2 reaches the vanilla two-loop model's average accuracy of 39.7 (34.7 without loops) at 4.9 ms decoding latency and 284M KV cache (batch size 4), against 9.4 ms and 560M for the vanilla two-loop model and 4.8 ms and 280M for the unlooped model. (Table 2; Section 3.1.2)

## Caveats

- The main results use in-house Seed-MoE models whose data and other training details are withheld; the open-source OLMo/OLMoE runs (1.2B dense and 1B/7B MoE at 400B tokens, plus a 100B-token dense ablation) test only L=2.
- Each model is trained and evaluated at one fixed loop count (L=2 or 3); the paper does not report running a different number of loops at inference.
- Parameters and training tokens are matched but compute is not; an L-loop PLT spends L times the per-token compute of the baseline (Table 1), and its latency advantage rests on decoding being memory-bound.
- CLP parallelizes decoding only; training stays serial along the loop dimension (Figure 4).
- Latency is per-token decoding latency on one GPU with FP8 attention, W4A8 linear layers and a 5000-token prefill; the latency and KV columns of Table 2 are at batch size 4.
- Hyperparameters of the in-house runs are not given, so the paper does not say whether the baseline was tuned separately.

## Authors

# MoR: Mixture-of-Recursions: Learning Dynamic Recursive Depths for Adaptive Token-Level Computation

English · [简体中文](../zh/2507.10524.md) · [Back to the list](../../README.md)

<sub>NeurIPS 2025 · arXiv 2507.10524 · 2025-07-14 · KAIST AI, Mila, Google Cloud, Google DeepMind, Google Research, Université de Montréal</sub>


> Routers give each token its own number of passes through a shared middle block, and each pass caches KV only for its active tokens; at equal training FLOPs MoR beats fixed-depth recursive baselines and often vanilla, with fewer parameters.

**Category**: Depth control · **Status**: draft (numbers not yet re-checked) · **Impact**: cites 217 · stars 652 · HF upvotes 74 · HN points 5

[paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.10524) · [code](https://github.com/raymin0223/mixture_of_recursions) · [weights](https://drive.google.com/drive/folders/1pYKJOu2aBGC-jgoWbfP6T_vqEYtUVxa4)

## Problem

Efficiency work usually targets either parameter sharing or adaptive computation. Recursive Transformers mostly apply one fixed depth to every token and keep a separate KV cache per depth, while early-exit methods need extra training stages and leave exited tokens without KV at deeper layers.

## Method

- Middle-Cycle sharing keeps the first and last layers unique and cycles one shared block of middle layers up to Nr times.
- Lightweight routers trained from scratch give each token its own recursion depth. Expert-choice picks the top-k tokens at every step with hierarchical filtering and adds an auxiliary BCE loss so the choice can be made causally at inference; token-choice assigns the depth once and uses a balancing loss.
- Recursion-wise caching stores KV at each step only for the tokens routed there and restricts attention to them; recursive KV sharing instead reuses the first step's KV at every step.
- Vanilla, fixed-depth recursive and MoR models (135M-1.7B base sizes, FineWeb-Edu, 2K context) are compared at equal training FLOPs (2e18, 5e18, 16.5e18) and at equal tokens (20B).

## Loop layout

| Facet | Value |
|---|---|
| Where the loop sits | middle core (prelude-core-coda) |
| Weight sharing | fully tied |
| Passes in training | learned / adaptive |
| Passes at test time | adaptive exit / routing |
| Input injection | none |
| KV cache | per-pass KV |
| Gradient through passes | full BPTT |
| Origin | trained from scratch |
| FFN | dense FFN |
| Attention in the loop | full attention |
| Passes (shared block) | train 1-3 per token, set by the router (Nr=3); test 1-3 per token, set by the router |

Middle-Cycle sharing on a Llama-style model keeps the first and last layers unique and applies one shared block up to Nr times (360M base with Nr=3 uses 1+10+1 unique layers; Nr=2 uses 1+15+1). Routers decide how many recursions each token gets. Expert-choice keeps the top-k tokens at each step (3/3, 2/3 and 1/3 of the tokens for Nr=3), and only tokens kept at step r can be kept at r+1; token-choice assigns each token its depth once. The router score scales the block output that is added to the residual. Each step caches KV only for its active tokens and attends only among them; a variant reuses the first recursion's KV at every step.

## Results

**360M base, FineWeb-Edu, 16.5e18 training FLOPs (tokens vary), Middle-Cycle sharing** · validation NLL / average few-shot accuracy · Table 3

| Variant | Value |
|---|---|
| Vanilla, 315M, 20B tokens | 2.7824 / 42.3 |
| Recursive Nr=2, 167M, 20B | 2.8079 / 42.6 |
| Recursive Nr=3, 118M, 20B | 2.8466 / 41.5 |
| Recursive Nr=4, 98M, 19B | 2.8781 / 41.0 |
| MoR expert Nr=2, 167M, 27B | 2.7511 / 43.1 |
| MoR expert Nr=3, 118M, 30B | 2.7925 / 42.6 |
| MoR expert Nr=4, 98M, 30B | 2.8204 / 41.6 |
| MoR token Nr=3, 118M, 30B | 2.9163 / 40.0 |
| MoR expert Nr=3, KV sharing, 118M, 31B | 2.7983 / 41.9 |

| Variant | Value |
|---|---|
| Vanilla | 16.5 / 2.7824 / 42.3 |
| MoR expert Nr=2 | 12.3 / 2.7749 / 42.9 |
| MoR expert Nr=3 | 11.0 / 2.8246 / 41.8 |
| MoR expert Nr=4 | 11.0 / 2.8519 / 41.5 |

| Variant | Value |
|---|---|
| Vanilla (Nr=1, 12 layers) | 2.9678 / 39.48 |
| MoR Nr=2 (1+10+1) | 2.9205 / 39.96 |
| MoR Nr=3 (1+10+1) | 2.9111 / 40.10 |

**Fixed-depth Recursive Transformers on the 360M base, Nr=3, 10B tokens; four parameter-sharing schemes** · validation NLL / average few-shot accuracy · Appendix F; Table 10

| Variant | Value |
|---|---|
| Vanilla, 32 layers, 315M | 2.8471 / 40.68 |
| Cycle, 10 layers, 98M | 2.9363 / 39.15 |
| Sequence, 10 layers, 98M | 3.0245 / 38.30 |
| Middle-Cycle, 1+10+1, 118M | 2.8760 / 40.82 |
| Middle-Sequence, 1+10+1, 118M | 2.9753 / 38.44 |

Cycle reuses the whole block in order [(0,1,2),(0,1,2),...]; Sequence repeats each layer back to back; the Middle variants keep the first and last layers unique.

## Other findings

- In Table 9, weight sharing alone (fixed-depth recursion) has higher validation NLL than vanilla at every size and budget. MoR has lower NLL than vanilla at 2e18 and 5e18 from the 360M base up, and at 16.5e18 only at the 1.7B base; at 135M it stays above vanilla. (Section 3.2; Appendix D; Table 9)
- At the 1.7B base with 68.5e18 FLOPs, vanilla averages 48.9 few-shot accuracy against 48.4 for the best MoR (expert, Nr=2); the authors say this might signal that the current MoR design is not suitable for scaling. (Appendix C.1; Table 7)
- With unique parameters fixed at 252M (730M base, Nr=3), Middle-Cycle with 1+8+1 layers (26 effective) beats Cycle with 10 layers (30 effective), with NLL 2.7552 vs 2.7573 and average accuracy 42.32 vs 41.90. (Appendix F; Table 11)
- At the 135M base, Cycle is slightly ahead of Middle-Cycle at Nr=2 (NLL 3.0071 vs 3.0330), while Middle-Cycle leads at Nr=3 and at the 360M base for both depths. In up-training from SmolLM checkpoints, both Middle strategies do better than the others in all settings. (Appendix F; Tables 10 and 12)
- At Nr=3, expert-choice routing beats token-choice (42.6% vs 40.0% average accuracy in Table 3). In the 10B-token ablation, recursive KV sharing raises training NLL for expert-choice MoR (2.8667 to 2.8895) but lowers it for token-choice MoR (2.9358 to 2.9155). (Section 3.1; Section 4.3; Tables 3 and 15)
- With continuous depth-wise batching at the 360M scale, every MoR variant decodes faster than vanilla, and MoR-4 reaches up to a 2.06× speedup at the maximum batch size, with a slight drop in quality. (Section 3.3; Figure 4a)
- Log-likelihood improves as the maximum recursion depth at inference is raised step by step up to the trained Nr (models with Nr=2, 3 and 4 at the 360M base); no run goes beyond the trained Nr. (Section 5.3; Figure 5c)

## Comparison

- **Baseline**: Vanilla Llama-style Transformer (315M non-embedding parameters at the 360M base) and fixed-depth Recursive Transformers with the same Middle-Cycle sharing (Nr=2-4).
- **Held fixed**: F (training FLOPs)
- **Differs**: N (unique parameters), D (training tokens), L (executed layers per token), KV (KV cache per token)
- **Baseline hyperparameters**: shared with the looped model
- **Headline claim**: At 16.5e18 training FLOPs, expert-choice MoR with Nr=2 reaches validation NLL 2.7511 and 43.1% average few-shot accuracy with 167M non-embedding parameters, against 2.7824 and 42.3% for the 315M vanilla model. At an equal 20B tokens it uses 25% fewer training FLOPs, 19% less training time and 25% less peak memory than vanilla. (Section 3.1; Table 3)

## Caveats

- Models go up to a 1.7B base (0.67B-0.87B unique non-embedding parameters for MoR) with 2K context, are trained only on FineWeb-Edu and are evaluated by NLL and six few-shot benchmarks; the authors leave models above 3B to future work (Section 7.1).
- The main comparison fixes training FLOPs, not parameters or tokens; MoR has fewer unique parameters and sees more tokens (27B-31B against 20B in Table 3).
- FLOPs are approximate forward-pass counts that leave out FlashAttention, normalization and non-linearities, and token-choice FLOPs assume perfect balancing (Appendix D).
- At the 135M base, and at the 1.7B base with 68.5e18 FLOPs, vanilla beats MoR (Section 3.2; Appendix C.1).
- Expert-choice top-k selection is non-causal during training; inference relies on an auxiliary loss to predict it, and the near-binary router outputs make top-k hard to change after training (Section 2.2.1; Section 7.1).
- Throughput is measured only at the 360M scale, generating from an empty prefix, and excludes the time spent caching and updating KV (Appendix E).
- Vanilla, recursive and MoR runs share one set of optimizer settings (learning rate 3e-3 in the released 360M configs); the paper reports no separate tuning.

|---|---|---|---|
| available | partial | partial | available |

- [Can later passes reuse one KV cache instead of keeping KV for every pass?](questions.md#shared-kv-across-passes) (partly)

## Authors

Sangmin Bae, Yujin Kim, Reza Bayat, Sungnyun Kim, Jiyoun Ha, Tal Schuster, Adam Fisch, Hrayr Harutyunyan, Ziwei Ji, Aaron Courville, Se-Young Yun


# Huginn: Scaling up Test-Time Compute with Latent Reasoning: A Recurrent Depth Approach

English · [简体中文](../zh/2502.05171.md) · [Back to the list](../../README.md)

<sub>arXiv 2502.05171 · 2025-02-07 · ELLIS Institute Tübingen, Max-Planck Institute for Intelligent Systems, Tübingen AI Center, University of Maryland, College Park, Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory</sub>


> Pretrain a 3.5B prelude-core-coda transformer with a randomly sampled number of core iterations, so test-time compute scales by iterating the core more.

**Category**: Architecture: where to loop, what to share · **Status**: draft (numbers not yet re-checked) · **Impact**: cites 623 · stars 1,000 · HF upvotes 162 · HN points 150

[paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.05171) · [code](https://github.com/seal-rg/recurrent-pretraining) · [weights](https://huggingface.co/tomg-group-umd/huginn-0125)

## Problem

Mainstream reasoning models scale test-time compute by generating more tokens in long chains of thought, which needs specialized training data and long context windows. The paper scales compute by iterating a recurrent block in latent space instead.

## Method

- Split a decoder-only transformer into a prelude, a weight-shared recurrent core and a coda. At every iteration the core receives the prelude output through an adapter on concat(state, prelude output); the first state is random.
- Sample the iteration count from a log-normal Poisson distribution with mean 32 (one count per micro-batch, synchronized across workers) and backpropagate through only the last 8 iterations.
- Train once at (2,4,2) with h=5280 on 800B tokens of public data weighted toward code and math, on 4096 AMD MI250X GPUs, with sandwich normalization (four RMSNorms per layer) and a scaled initialization.
- At inference the iteration count is free; the paper also tries zero-shot per-token early exit, KV-cache sharing, continuous-CoT warm starts and self-speculative decoding.

## Loop layout

| Facet | Value |
|---|---|
| Where the loop sits | middle core (prelude-core-coda) |
| Weight sharing | fully tied |
| Passes in training | sampled |
| Passes at test time | can run more passes than trained |
| Input injection | concat + projection |
| KV cache | per-pass KV |
| Gradient through passes | truncated (last k passes) |
| Origin | trained from scratch |
| FFN | dense FFN |
| Attention in the loop | full attention |
| Passes (R) | train log-normal Poisson, mean 32; test 1-64 (32 in most tables) |
| Backprop (R) | last 8 |

Huginn-0125 has 8 distinct layers in a (2,4,2) layout with hidden size 5280 and 55 heads of size 96. The core starts with an adapter that maps the concatenation of the state and the prelude output from 2h to h, and the first state is random noise. At r=32 the model unrolls to 132 effective layers. Small ablation models use (1,4,1) with h=1024.

## Results

**3.5B parameters, both models at 180B tokens (0.18T), same data and setup** · ARC-C | HellaSwag | GSM8K CoT · Table 4

| Variant | Value |
|---|---|
| Fixed-depth baseline (one core pass) | 26.96 \| 37.34 \| 1.82/2.20 |
| Recurrent model, r=32 | 29.18 \| 48.80 \| 9.02/10.24 |
| Recurrent model, r=1 | 23.72 \| 29.19 \| 0.00/0.15 |

GSM8K CoT pairs are copied as printed; the Table 2 caption says the paper reports flexible and strict extract.

**Huginn-0125 (3.5B, 800B tokens), lm-eval zero-shot at different test-time recurrences r** · ARC-C | HellaSwag | MMLU · Table 1 (arXiv v2); Table 4 (r=1 row)

| Variant | Value |
|---|---|
| r=1 | 24.06 \| 29.34 \| 23.60 |
| r=4 | 27.99 \| 43.46 \| 23.39 |
| r=8 | 35.15 \| 58.54 \| 25.29 |
| r=16 | 37.71 \| 64.67 \| 31.25 |
| r=32 | 38.23 \| 65.21 \| 31.38 |

arXiv v1 printed different values in the r=4, 8 and 16 rows of Table 1; these are the v2 values.

**Huginn-0125 at r=32 next to fixed-depth open models** · GSM8K | GSM8K CoT | Minerva MATH · Table 2

| Variant | Value |
|---|---|
| Huginn-0125, with system prompt | 24.87/38.13 \| 34.80/42.08 \| 11.24 |
| Huginn-0125, without system prompt | 28.05/28.20 \| 32.60/34.57 \| 12.58 |
| OLMo-7B-0724 | 28.66/28.73 \| 28.89/28.89 \| 5.62 |
| OLMo-2-1124-7B | 66.72/66.79 \| 61.94/66.19 \| 19.08 |

**Huginn-0125, first-turn MT-Bench, inference schemes used zero-shot** · MT-Bench score (standard error) · Table 6; Sections 6.1-6.2

| Variant | Value |
|---|---|
| baseline, 32 iterations | 5.662 (0.388) |
| baseline, 64 iterations | 5.693 (0.386) |
| KL exit, t=5×10^-4 | 5.562 (0.389) |
| cache compression, s=4 | 5.856 (0.395) |
| cache compression, s=8 | 5.631 (0.384) |
| cache compression, s=16 | 5.687 (0.402) |

s is the per-token KV-cache budget in recurrence steps. The paper states no difference from the baseline is statistically significant.

## Other findings

- Evaluated with one recurrence, the model barely changes between the 180B and 800B checkpoints (ARC-C 23.72 and 24.06); the authors conclude that later gains sit in the recurrent iterations, not in the prelude or coda. (Section 5.3; Table 4)
- Useful depth depends on task and context. HellaSwag is near its peak at 8 recurrences; ARC-C saturates around 8-12 iterations with no few-shot examples, around 20 with 1 example and around 32 with 25-50 examples. (Section 5.3; Figures 7 and 9)
- Tested at r=64 (training mean 32), an EMA of the last 75 checkpoints reaches 47.23% flexible (38.59% strict) on GSM8K. (Section 5.4)
- In ablations, a core block that takes the step index as input interacted badly with path independence and gave models that cannot extrapolate; adding noise at each step did not help. (Section 3.1 (Remark 3.1))
- Two earlier large-scale runs failed. In one, all tokens collapsed to the same hidden state; in the other, the model learned to ignore the recurrent state, with the same validation perplexity at 1 or 32 recurrences. The successful run used sandwich norms and a peak learning rate of 4×10^-5. (Section 4.3; Figure 5)

## Comparison

- **Baseline**: A fixed-depth twin with the same architecture, data and training setup that passes through the core block once, trained for 180B tokens (256 nodes, batch size 2 per GPU).
- **Held fixed**: N (unique parameters), D (training tokens)
- **Differs**: F (training FLOPs), L (executed layers per token)
- **Baseline hyperparameters**: shared with the looped model
- **Headline claim**: The 3.5B model trained on 800B tokens improves on reasoning benchmarks as test-time recurrence grows, up to a computation load equivalent to 50B parameters. At 180B tokens and r=32 it scores 9.02/10.24 on GSM8K CoT against 1.82/2.20 for the fixed-depth twin, which the paper calls 5 times better. (Abstract; Section 5.3; Table 4)

## Caveats

- A single large run with 3.5B parameters and 800B tokens, on a data mixture the authors could not ablate and with a constant learning rate that was never cooled down (47000 steps).
- The looped-vs-fixed-depth comparison exists only at 180B tokens. It matches parameters and tokens but not compute, since the baseline passes through the core once.
- The comparisons with Amber, Pythia, OLMo and StarCoder2 models (Tables 1-3) are not matched in parameters, tokens or data.
- Training uses 4096-token sequences and backpropagates through only the last 8 core iterations.
- Early exit, KV-cache sharing and continuous CoT are zero-shot uses of a model not trained for them, measured only on first-turn MT-Bench, where the differences are not statistically significant (Table 6). Self-speculative decoding has no reported measurements.

# Open questions

English · [简体中文](../zh/questions.md) · [Back to the list](../../README.md)

## <a id="extra-passes-at-test-time"></a>Does running more passes at test time than in training keep improving quality?

**mixed** · updated 2026-11-23

Models trained with a sampled or variable number of passes stay flat or improve slightly beyond the training depth, and their gains level off near the training mean. Ouro, trained with 4 steps and learned exits rather than sampled depth, loses accuracy at 5-8 steps. No source trains the same model both ways, so the role of sampled-depth training is not isolated.

| Paper | Stance | Setting | Finding | Ref |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| [Huginn](2502.05171.md) | partly | 3.5B dense, 800B tokens, passes sampled with mean 32 | First-turn MT-Bench is 5.693 at 64 iterations and 5.662 at 32, a difference the paper calls not significant. ARC-C saturates around 8-12 iterations without few-shot examples and around 32 with 25-50 examples. | Table 6; Section 5.3; Figures 7 and 9 |
| [Parcae](2604.12946.md) | partly | 350M (RDM setup) trained with mean 8 passes sampled per sequence; 140M-1.3B models for the saturation result | Validation PPL is 10.09 at T=8 and 10.11 at T=16. Run at up to twice the training mean, the 140M-1.3B models' gains plateau near T = μ_rec. | Table 8; Section 5.3; Figure 7 |
| [Looped CED](2611.13378.md) | partly | 150M CED, 6.0B tokens, rounds sampled from max(1, Poisson(8)) | Running 12 or 16 rounds instead of 8 lowers BPB by at most 0.0004 and never raises it (0.8465 at T=8, 0.8462 at T=12 and 16). | Appendix F; Table 9 |
| [Retrofitted Recurrence](2511.07384.md) | partly | TinyLlama-1.1B retrofitted to (4,8,4), about 50B math tokens | Trained with mean recurrence 4, the model scores 38.0 on GSM8K at test recurrence 4 and 37.9 at 32; trained with mean 16, it scores 43.4 at test recurrence 16 and 43.7 at 32. | Table 3 |
| [Inkling 2 Mini](tml-inkling-2-mini.md) | partly | TML-d24-varloop-research, 26.4B total / 3.4B active MoE, trained with 1-5 passes | Never trained with more than five passes, it keeps a no-CoT 50% time horizon of 40 s at ten passes against 42 s at five, and on N-Hop Lookup it keeps improving out to ten loops. | No-CoT capabilities; figures "No-CoT time horizons" and "N-Hop Lookup" |
| [Ouro (LoopLM)](2510.25741.md) | against | Ouro 1.4B and 2.6B, 7.7T tokens, trained with 4 recurrent steps (8 in the first stage) and learned exit gates | MMLU falls from 67.45 at T=4 to 64.49 at T=8 for the 1.4B model and from 74.60 to 72.24 for the 2.6B model; AIME 2024 for the 1.4B Thinking model falls from 65.00 at T=4 to 38.67 at T=8. Safety on HEx-PHI keeps improving through the extrapolated steps. | Tables 10-13; Section 7.1; Figure 8a |

## <a id="loop-placement"></a>Where in the stack should the loop sit?

**consistent** · updated 2026-11-25

Every comparison favors looping lower or middle layers over the whole stack or the top layers, and in layouts with a shared global KV the loop should include the layers that produce it. The comparisons come from models of 1.7B parameters or less (the 1.7B one finetuned from a pretrained model), or from runs whose sizes are not given.

| Paper | Stance | Setting | Finding | Ref |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| [SMELT](2609.01343.md) | supports | 200M MoE, FLOPs, parameters and KV matched, two passes | Looping the middle 6 of 12 layers gives validation loss 1.9257 against 1.9322 for looping all 12 (S ≈ 85%), and every span tested beats the unlooped Baseline (1.9445). DCLM Core at S ≈ 95% peaks at the 67% span instead. | Table 3; Section 3.3 |
| [Inkling 2 Mini](tml-inkling-2-mini.md) | supports | Scaling-ladder runs, three passes, equal training compute; model sizes not given | Looping the middle 12 layers beat looping the last 12 on 27 of 28 evaluations; a no-loop baseline would need an estimated 1.51-1.91x the compute to match the middle loop, against 1.24-1.36x for the last loop. | Looping design; figure "Compute-equivalent gain by loop position" |
| [Looped CED](2611.13378.md) | supports | 150M CED, 6.0B and 29.6B tokens | Looping encoder layers L2-5, which contain the global KV source, reaches 0.8468 BPB against 0.8648 for looping decoder layers L7-10 (no loop 0.8716); after 29.6B tokens the decoder loop captures only 38% of the encoder loop's improvement. | Table 1; Table 2 |
| [YOCO-U](2604.01220.md) | supports | 1.3B dense, 20B tokens | Looping the self-decoder averages 48.25 against 47.34 for looping the cross-decoder. At about 2x FLOPs, looping the whole 20-layer Transformer twice averages 47.8 against 48.3 for RINS and YOCO-U. | Table 5; Table 3 |
| [MoR](2507.10524.md) | partly | Fixed-depth recursive models; 730M base with unique parameters fixed at 252M (Nr=3), and 135M base (Nr=2) | Keeping the first and last layers unshared (Middle-Cycle, 1+8+1) beats cycling the whole stack (Cycle, 10 layers) at 252M unique parameters, NLL 2.7552 vs 2.7573 and accuracy 42.32 vs 41.90; at the 135M base with Nr=2, Cycle is slightly ahead (3.0071 vs 3.0330). | Appendix F; Tables 10-11 |
| [LoopRes](2611.31094.md) | supports | Qwen3-1.7B-Base finetuned on 3.1B tokens of math and code SFT data, 2x compute | For Huginn + AttnRes, looping the middle 14 of 28 layers three times averages 53.9 on seven math and code benchmarks, against 50.9 for looping all layers twice at the same 2x compute. | Appendix C.1; Table 12 |

## <a id="more-passes-fixed-compute"></a>With training compute held fixed, do more passes help?

**mixed** · updated 2026-11-23

On language modeling at the budgets tested, SMELT and MoR find two passes better than three or four with FLOPs fixed, and in Ouro the gap to untied models of the same executed depth grows with the step count. Other results point the other way: Parcae's compute-optimal number of passes rises with the training budget, deeper training recurrence pays off per training FLOP for two of three retrofitted model families, and on Ouro's synthetic Mano task more passes of fewer layers win at the same executed depth.

| Paper | Stance | Setting | Finding | Ref |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| [SMELT](2609.01343.md) | against | 200M MoE, S ≈ 85%, FLOPs, parameters and KV matched (more passes force a narrower model) | Validation loss is 1.9257 at 2 passes, 1.9385 at 3 and 1.9360 at 4; DCLM Core is 27.57, 27.15 and 27.30. | Table 5; Section 3.5 |
| [MoR](2507.10524.md) | against | 360M base, 16.5e18 training FLOPs; more recursions mean fewer unique parameters (167M, 118M, 98M) | Expert-choice MoR reaches validation NLL 2.7511 at Nr=2, 2.7925 at Nr=3 and 2.8204 at Nr=4; fixed-depth recursion gives 2.8079, 2.8466 and 2.8781 (vanilla 2.7824). | Table 3 |
| [Ouro (LoopLM)](2510.25741.md) | against | 53M-1.36B, 20B FineWeb-Edu tokens; untied model with the same executed depth and more unique parameters | The untied model scores higher in every case and the gap grows with the step count; at 1.3B the average benchmark gap is 0.017 at 2 steps and 0.025 at 4. | Appendix D.1; Table 18 |
| [Ouro (LoopLM)](2510.25741.md) | supports | Synthetic Mano task (modular arithmetic), 12 executed layers in every layout, unique parameters differ | At maximum expression length 24, 3 layers looped 4 times reach 92.2 exact-match accuracy, against 78.0 for 2 layers x 6, 35.1 for 6 layers x 2 and 34.8 for 12 unlooped layers. | Section 6.2; Figure 6 (right) |
| [Parcae](2604.12946.md) | partly | 140M and 370M, parameters and training FLOPs fixed (tokens shrink as passes grow) | The compute-optimal mean recurrence rises with the budget, from 2 at 1x10^18 FLOPs to 10 at 64x10^18 for 140M, following a power law with exponent about 0.40; at some small budgets fixed depth scores higher Core (10.5 vs 9.0 at 2x10^18 FLOPs). | Table 6; Section 5.2; Figure 5 |
| [Retrofitted Recurrence](2511.07384.md) | partly | 1B-class models retrofitted from TinyLlama, OLMo and Llama, about 50B math tokens | Per training FLOP, larger training recurrences give a larger GSM8K gain for OLMo and Llama but not for TinyLlama. | Section 4.3.2; Figure 20 |

## <a id="shared-kv-across-passes"></a>Can later passes reuse one KV cache instead of keeping KV for every pass?

**mixed** · updated 2026-11-23

Reusing the last pass's KV works when the model is trained for it or when it is done only during decoding, while reusing the first pass's KV alone costs accuracy unless a local window is added. Looped CED loses nothing with last-round KV under sampled-depth training but fails with fixed depth, Ouro keeps quality with last-step KV in decoding but not in prefill, and PLT needs a gated sliding window on top of first-pass KV sharing.

| Paper | Stance | Setting | Finding | Ref |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| [Looped CED](2611.13378.md) | partly | 150M CED, 6.0B tokens, exact fp32 token-by-token decoding at T=8 | With sampled-depth training, last-round KV changes BPB by -0.0002 relative to per-round KV; with fixed-depth training it adds +0.0317. | Table 3 |
| [Ouro (LoopLM)](2510.25741.md) | partly | Ouro 1.4B, KV reuse during decoding only | Keeping only the last step's KV gives GSM8K 78.85 and MATH-500 80.40 against 78.92 and 82.40 with all four caches, at 4.00x less memory; first-step-only KV drops to 18.73 and 8.43, and reusing KV during prefill costs more than 10 points on GSM8K. | Section 5.4.2; Table 14 |
| [PLT](2510.24824.md) | partly | 680M activated / 13B total MoE, 150B tokens | Sharing the first loop's KV halves the KV cache (560M to 280M) but lowers average accuracy from 39.6 to 36.2; adding gated SWA with a 64-token window restores 39.7 at 284M. | Table 2 |
| [YOCO-U](2604.01220.md) | supports | 1.3B dense, 20B tokens | Looping the cross-decoder while it keeps reading the one shared global KV averages 47.34, against 46.41 when those layers use their own self-attention KV instead. | Table 5; Section 4.3 |
| [MoR](2507.10524.md) | partly | 360M-base family, 10B FineWeb-Edu tokens | Recursive KV sharing, which reuses the first recursion's KV, raises validation NLL for expert-choice MoR from 2.8667 to 2.8895 but lowers it for token-choice MoR from 2.9358 to 2.9155. | Section 4.3; Table 15 |
| [Huginn](2502.05171.md) | supports | Huginn 3.5B, zero-shot (not trained for it), first-turn MT-Bench | Capping the per-token KV cache at s=4, 8 or 16 recurrence steps scores 5.856, 5.631 and 5.687 against 5.662 for the full cache at 32 iterations; the paper finds no significant difference. | Table 6; Section 6.2 |
